articles.content: For post-secondary students, every new academic year inevitably comes with tuition bills, textbook costs and a long list of student fees, as well as mandatory health plans . Students are locked into a number of plans covering outpatient prescription drugs, dental, extended health and virtual health care, but they’re not allowed to opt out of their school plans without comparable private insurance. These plans make Ontario college and university students under age 25 ineligible for the Ontario Health Insurance Plan Plus (OHIP+) , which covers nearly 6,000 medications at no out-of-pocket cost. Ontario’s Liberal government introduced OHIP+ in January 2018, providing free prescription drug coverage to eligible residents under 25, regardless of private insurance. In April 2019, Premier Doug Ford’s Conservative government restricted OHIP+ to cover only those who did not otherwise have private coverage . As OHIP coverage cannot be used to opt out of school plans, thousands of post-secondary students lost access to Ontario’s public drug program. To examine how Ontario post-secondary students may have been affected by this sudden change, we reviewed prescription drug plans across colleges and universities. We documented all cost-sharing components (for example, deductible, co-insurance, co-payment, dispensing fees and annual limits), specific coverage for contraceptives and exclusions . We then compared students’ coverage to the coverage available under OHIP. Variations in plans We identified substantial variation in prescription drug coverage across university and college student health plans, resulting in important inequities. There were significant disparities in cost-sharing and contraceptive coverage. Students were responsible for paying anywhere from zero per cent to 50 per cent of their prescription costs, most commonly 20 per cent. Annual coverage limits ranged from $250 to $12,500. Additionally, colleges in northern Ontario generally offered less comprehensive coverage and imposed more restrictive reimbursement criteria. Notably, none of the plans sponsored by student unions compared favourably with coverage available through OHIP. Contraceptive coverage varied considerably across institutions. Some plans covered oral contraceptives but excluded other methods such as devices and implants. Others imposed product-specific reimbursement limits, while some provided no contraceptive coverage at all. These gaps are especially concerning given that the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada identifies intrauterine devices as a first-line contraceptive option for adolescents and young adults. This illustrates the disconnect between evidence-based clinical guidelines and private insurance coverage policies. Many coverage restrictions affect conditions that already carry significant stigma, particularly among young adults. Treatments for smoking cessation, obesity, acne, infertility and erectile dysfunction were frequently excluded from coverage, subject to reimbursement caps or otherwise restricted. Such limitations may create additional barriers to care, as students may be reluctant to seek treatment because of financial concerns, stigma or both. Smoking cessation therapies were frequently excluded from student health plan coverage. In contrast, OHIP provides coverage for prescription smoking cessation medications for individuals aged 18 years and older, as well as up to one year of pharmacist-led smoking cessation counselling. In 2020, the United States Surgeon General highlighted the critical role of insurance coverage in supporting smoking cessation, stating: “Insurance coverage for smoking cessation treatment that is comprehensive, barrier-free, and widely promoted increases the use of these treatment services, leads to higher rates of successful quitting, and is cost-effective.” Impact on health and access to care Higher prescription drug costs can have important consequences for students’ health and access to care. Research from Canada and internationally consistently shows that people are more likely to use medications when they have insurance and face lower out-of-pocket costs. Conversely, losing insurance or facing higher costs can reduce medication use. A recent study in JAMA Pediatrics found that the introduction of universal coverage in Ontario in 2018 led to increases in contraceptive dispensations and decreases after restrictions were introduced. Beyond the equity and health implications of the April 2019 changes to Ontario’s public drug program, important efficiency concerns also arise. Public drug insurance programs such as OHIP are generally more efficient than private insurance mechanisms, including post-secondary student plans, in collecting revenue, sharing financial risk and administering coverage. As a result, public systems can often deliver comparable or more comprehensive coverage at a lower overall cost than fragmented private insurance arrangements. The modest reductions in government spending associated with the 2019 cuts are unlikely to offset the additional costs imposed on Ontario residents. Given the inherent and increasing inefficiencies of private insurance, including higher administrative expenses and less effective risk pooling , shifting coverage from the public to the private sector is likely to increase overall system costs and lead to higher premiums for students and their families. articles.content: Children with lifelong diseases and their families often seek answers about their illness from the internet. However, filtering out what is trustworthy information and what is not, and struggling to understand medical jargon, can leave children, teens and parents at risk of accepting unreliable information. That can be detrimental to care. Digital health literacy is the ability to find, evaluate and use electronic health information to help manage a health problem. People with higher levels of digital health literacy live healthier lives and make better health-related choices . To better understand how teens with chronic diseases and their caregivers navigate online health information, our pediatric rheumatology research team at the University of Saskatchewan spoke with adolescents living with chronic arthritis and related rheumatic diseases , along with their caregivers, to better understand how they access, evaluate and use online health information. The results from the interviews were recently published in the journal Children . While it wasn’t a surprise that all the teens and caregivers who were interviewed used the internet and technology for health support, as most Canadians do , there was considerable variability in how beneficial the information was for their health care. Information and misinformation Online health misinformation is widespread, and identifying what is trustworthy information can be difficult. Both adolescents and caregivers in our study said they often relied on common internet icons as indicators of the trustworthiness of online health information. These include the HTTPS padlock icon and the social media blue check mark. However, many did not realize that the padlock icon means secure data transfer and the check mark icon indicates a verified account, but neither symbol has any relevance to the reliability of the online health information. Read more: The vast majority of us have no idea what the padlock icon on our internet browser is – and it’s putting us at risk Adolescents and caregivers said they used online health information to answer “quick little questions,” as an alternative to “bothering” their health-care providers for an answer. Adolescents looked for online health information relating to how to manage symptoms and prepare for treatments, like dealing with a fear of needles. Caregivers looked for online health information to reassure themselves that their decisions about their child’s management are supported by reliable evidence and to reduce anxiety over their child’s health. However, both teens and caregivers reported they often can’t find the answers they’re looking for. This is because some of the answers don’t exist yet, such as the long-term effects of newer medications. Another problem identified was that online health information specifically for adolescents is limited. Most existing online health information is either geared toward younger children or is too complicated to understand. Role of medical teams As concerning as these findings are, the study found that the medical teams served as an important safety net for protecting patients and caregivers from misinformation. Most participants spoke of how they trust their medical teams. They described how they discuss online health information with their care providers before making health decisions. Read more: Online wellness content: 3 ways to tell evidence-based health information from pseudoscience The study showed that teens with rheumatic diseases and their caregivers confront barriers to developing high levels of digital health literacy while seeking online health information. These barriers include: An inability to confidently distinguish online health misinformation from reliable information, Eeliance on false indicators of online health information trustworthiness, and Misplaced trust in online health information by individuals inappropriately identifying as a medical doctor. Health-care providers, alongside children and teens with chronic diseases and their caregivers, should develop resources to support improving digital health literacy for patients and families and create online health information suitable for children, adolescents and their caregivers. Health-care teams should provide age-appropriate “prescriptions” that recommend strategies for accessing, interpreting and using reliable sources of online health information. articles.content: Aging can seem like a negative process, one that causes our bodies to slow down and deteriorate. The aging brain, however, retains remarkable resilience. And some of the changes that occur within the aging brain are actually helpful adaptations. Our recent research study reveals this process of adaptation — showing that the brains of healthy older adults may cope better with lack of sleep than those of younger adults . Neuroplasticity in older age In this study, we investigated the neuroplasticity of human brain networks across the lifespan. Neuroplasticity refers to the brain’s extraordinary ability to change , particularly through the reorganization of brain connections. The most extreme periods of neuroplasticity occur during brain development in childhood , adolescence and the transition to early adulthood . However, the healthy brain retains its neuroplasticity throughout the lifespan, and undergoes periods of pronounced reorganization even in older age . Aging brains face many challenges, including cortical thinning or brain shrinkage , white matter demyelination and cognitive decline . As a result, many researchers treat aging as a proxy for purely negative brain changes. Our research goes against this trend by identifying multiple ways in which brain changes may actually be helpful adaptations to the challenges of aging. Preserving function for tomorrow Previous research has suggested that older adults do not suffer as badly from the negative effects of minimal sleep — decreased cognitive ability and mood — as younger adults do. In our study, we wanted to understand what is happening in the brain to cause this. So we compared the brains of younger adults (20-30 years) and older adults (65-75 years) after experiencing a full night of sleep and a night with only three hours of sleep. We found that part of the older brain’s functional connectivity responded in the opposite way to the brains of younger adults. After a night with only three hours of sleep, older adult brains reduced connections in a way that increased modularity . That is, their brain regions formed more local modules, with a small number of global connections between modules. Conversely, younger adult brains showed decreased modularity . Modularity is an efficient network organization associated with better cognitive outcomes . Our research suggests the brain may compensate for age-related changes by responding to short-term sleep loss in an adaptive way, preserving efficient brain function the next day. Strengthening local connections These findings complement our broader program of research identifying long-term reorganizations of brain networks that support cognitive outcomes in older age. Interestingly, these are distinct from the connectivity patterns that are beneficial for younger adults. We continue to see a recurring theme: The healthy brain seems to adapt to white matter demyelination with age by relying less on longer global connections and instead strengthening local connectivity . This growing program of research speaks to the healthy aging brain’s resilience to challenges, where neuroplasticity supports reorganization and adaptation. Sleep while you are young How do we help to promote these neuroplastic adaptations? One way is through physical activity . Another important lifestyle factor is getting a healthy amount of sleep throughout one’s life . Recent research has shown that sleep can directly affect both the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and how quickly it progresses . The amyloid and tau proteins that accumulate in brains with Alzheimer’s disease accumulate at a faster rate when sleep is disrupted . Researchers estimate that 15 per cent of Alzheimer’s disease cases could be prevented by identifying people with poor sleep quality and intervening to promote better sleep. The disease processes that cause Alzheimer’s disease develop for decades before an individual will experience memory loss and be diagnosed with dementia , so there is a large window of opportunity to detect and treat the disease and prevent cognitive decline. articles.content: The latest episode of Saturday Night Live (SNL) featured a viral comedy sketch in which a series of men confidently explain that their sisters will shoulder the burden of caring for their aging parents. The sketch is funny because it’s so familiar. In just three minutes of satire, it captures a reality many women know all too well: when parents need care, daughters are often expected to step in while sons step aside. articles.content: Typical cases of 'rebirth syndrome' encompass narrative, biological, emotional and behavioural components. Painting: Luke Fildes's 'The Doctor' ( Wikimedia Commons) For more than 60 years, the University of Virginia’s Division of Perceptual Studies (DOPS) has collected information about children who seemingly recall past lives. Its digitized database contains 2,254 records with more than 200 variables for each case. Most of these children provided enough detail to unambiguously identify a previous identity. Based on 1,678 matched cases (released as open data ), DOPS researchers found that an unexpected death was associated with a shorter “intermission period” before rebirth. This study has generated wide coverage in English and Spanish media . Most news outlets highlight these findings as “striking.” However, as a causal inference specialist, I think the pattern in the DOPS study might reflect something much simpler and less exciting: selection bias. Unexpected deaths are more likely to be newsworthy. News archives, in turn, are the type of source that DOPS researchers use to identify potential matches. This selection effect builds up over time and can easily explain the main study findings. The bullfighter K’s story is not part of the DOPS database, but is typical of children’s statements about past lives. I learned about it through K’s mother, Made. She shared her story online after viewing a social media reel about reincarnation. I reached out to Made because very few cases had been studied in Latin America; none in my native Ecuador. Made told me that K was three years old when he sat on his bed and spontaneously began telling Made and her husband about having lived as a bullfighter in Spain. K told them he remembered a bull stuck its horn in his stomach. “Here,” he said, lifting his T-shirt and putting his finger above the left hip, where he has a birthmark. The bull goring had caused him severe pain and he was taken to the hospital. “Then I died, and after that I woke up with you two,” Made recalls him saying. Birthmarks or birth defects are not unheard of among children who seemingly recall past lives. However, a deep emotional involvement is the key component. Made says that after explaining his death, K talked about his previous family and how much he missed them. “He had tears in his eyes when he talked about his other mum,” Made told me. Both of K’s parents were dumbfounded, as neither had ever entertained the idea that reincarnation was real. “My husband is Catholic and I am evangelical Christian,” Made says. At the time — nine years ago — the family lived in Quito, Ecuador, and neither parent had ever visited Spain. According to them, there had been no references to that country, let alone bullfighting, as they only allowed K to watch age-appropriate content. Biology and memory Biology does not provide straight answers about children who seemingly recall past lives, but the field is exploring a question relevant to it: what mechanisms allow for memory transmission outside of the brain and between generations? Biologist Michael Levin started experimenting with Planaria — flatworms with a remarkable ability to regenerate severed parts — because he wanted to know if they would retain memories in a regenerated head. These invertebrates have most of the same neurotransmitters humans do and have become an influential model for the study of the brain. Levin conducted a simple experiment that took advantage of the planaria’s proclivity to always examine unknown terrain. The results showed that the worms seemed to remember the terrain, even though Levin had chopped their entire heads off. The study suggests “that some trace of memory is stored in locations distributed beyond the brain.” Levin later suggested that researchers should look at epigenetic mechanisms (factors that influence gene expression), “but this alone doesn’t begin to explain it.” In a recent interview , DOPS researcher Philip Cozzolino shared researchers’ plans to search for epigenetic signatures in children who claim to recall a past life, particularly among those who seem to behave as if they have survived trauma. In a 2005 review of a book about children’s past life memories, Levin discussed the flatworm model in that context, noting that it “doesn’t take us all the way to a discarnate entity, and may or may not apply to higher vertebrates, but it provides a foot-hold to begin, giving biologists an experimentally tractable entry-point into the process of how information could be imposed on a forming brain from outside the brain.” In 2023, a study conducted on roundworms ( C. Elegans ) suggested that associative memories may be transferred across generations. More recently, biologist Martha R. Weiss held an online seminar about butterflies’ learning and memory. She shared the findings of her youngest-ever collaborator — 10-year-old Jo Nagai — who had just confirmed that his butterflies recalled associations they had learned as caterpillars. Then, he pushed the study further. Weiss reported that Jo “found persistence of memory into the next generation. And right now we are writing up his results for publication.” Addressing selection bias We know there are cases out there that have never been studied because people like Made didn’t approach anyone. These cases involve people who share their stories online but are not part of any database. Looking at the same social media reel that Made saw, you could see dozens of parents claiming at least some partial resemblance to the prototypical case of “ rebirth syndrome ” that encompasses narrative, biological, emotional and behavioural components. There is a straightforward way to address selection bias. Rather than waiting for families to approach researchers when a child reports a troubling memory, researchers could directly ask all families instead. Talking to a full crowd at the Behind and Beyond the Brain Symposium , which I attended in April 2026, former DOPS director Jim Tucker shared some preliminary results. They started with a convenience sample of mothers in Virginia. When Tucker looked at the numbers, the proportion was so high he thought something had gone wrong. DOPS then developed an 11-item assessment and established a threshold to make sure the measure was robust. Then, they improved the target population. Using a nationally representative sample of English-speaking mothers in the United States with children ages 5 to 13 (whom they have raised since the child was 3), DOPS researchers found that 6.9 per cent of mothers reported having the type of emotionally meaningful interaction Made had with K. The path forward Psychological research into people who claim to remember past lives has historically studied only a very small number of individuals. Not only due to stigma (you can start with the intention of disproving the phenomena ) but precisely because it was assumed the cases were extremely rare. The high prevalence of “rebirth syndrome” opens the door to population-level studies. Developmental cohorts — study designs that regularly ask parents about many aspects of a child’s life over time — could firmly establish associations between these memories and many other facets of the human psyche. DOPS, for example, found that people who recall past lives as the opposite sex are significantly more likely to display gender non-conforming traits . I look forward to the day when researchers embrace the study of the “rebirth” phenomenon (even if they ultimately attribute it to fantasy). Taking a first step could be as simple as incorporating DOPS’ 11-item assessment into their existing studies. Such a small choice could reshape not only how we understand the interplay between memory and biology, but also our understanding of where we come from, the nature of mind and the deeper questions about human existence that science has rarely had the opportunity to explore. articles.content: Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide — a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and body weight — have become household names and important pillars in obesity management for the medical profession. Research has shown GLP-1 medications reduce body weight by an average of 15 per cent when used weekly for 68 weeks and combined with lifestyle interventions. This is because semaglutide acts on the brain to increase the feeling of fullness and to decrease appetite. These medications don’t work the same way for everyone, however. Our multidisciplinary research team at the University of Alberta is working to improve obesity care for people of all ages and to understand why some people respond better to semaglutide than others, and how their weight loss can be maintained over time. We are investigating the role of energy metabolism as a potentially important piece in a complex puzzle. The challenge of metabolic adaptation Research has shown semaglutide medications to improve quality of life , blood markers such as sugar or cholesterol , strength and overall health. Weight loss is only one measure of how well they work. We are exploring whether people’s responses to these medications could lie in individual factors such as genetics, metabolism, body composition, lifestyle, microbiota, associated diseases, age and sex. Obesity medication is an important pillar of obesity management and should be monitored as part of a comprehensive, multidisciplinary approach to care. (Obesity Canada) , CC BY-NC-ND Energy metabolism may also be an important piece of this puzzle. This is a measure of the total calories consumed (in) and the total calories burned (out). We burn calories all the time: for vital processes like breathing and thinking, physical activities like going to the gym and the everyday act of digesting food. When we lose weight, our bodies naturally need less energy. But sometimes, the body goes into an extra “energy-saving mode,” burning even fewer calories than we would expect. This is called metabolic adaptation, or adaptive thermogenesis . Think of it like a light bulb that automatically dims to save electricity. This is one reason why losing weight can become more difficult over time, sometimes leading to a weight-loss plateau. Emerging areas of research Changes in body weight and composition (the amount of fat and fat-free mass in our bodies) play an important role in energy metabolism. Both fat and fat-free mass use energy, even when we are resting. As we lose these tissues, our bodies naturally burn fewer calories. Researchers are still trying to understand whether weight-loss medications influence these processes differently. If we can understand how our bodies use energy during and after weight loss, this could help us develop better strategies for maintaining weight loss over the long term. We published a recent review of studies investigating the effects of GLP-1 therapies on energy utilization . We found a few studies exploring how semaglutide affects resting energy use, with findings that were neutral or inconclusive. The question of how semaglutide impacts energy use is an emerging area of study, and remains an open question for exploration. Personalized approaches to obesity At the University of Alberta, we have a gold-standard method to measure energy utilization called a whole-room indirect calorimeter . This is a rare research facility and is similar to a hotel suite that can precisely measure each component of energy use . This room can isolate the effects of changes in someone’s calorie burning at rest, after eating and during exercise. We are currently recruiting research participants with blood sugar regulation issues, such as insulin resistance or diabetes, who are about to start semaglutide treatment. We will follow their weight loss journey over six months to investigate changes in body weight and composition, and energy utilization using sophisticated approaches. Understanding how semaglutide influences energy use and body composition, and how these changes interact, could be an important step toward explaining why individuals respond differently to weight-loss treatment. This will allow us to contribute to more personalized approaches to obesity and Type 2 diabetes management in the future. Having a better understanding of how energy use changes with semaglutide-induced weight loss will also help us to better anticipate potential non-responders (people who do not lose weight) and offer alternative treatments sooner in their health journey. Lifestyle changes for success Importantly, current evidence suggests that if you are taking semaglutide or considering starting treatment, you should make a few lifestyle changes. Current guidelines recommend people using GLP-1 medications to engage in resistance exercise to optimize their body composition for the best results. (Obesity Canada) , CC BY-NC-ND These include improving your nutrition by increasing protein intake and prioritizing fresh foods , such as fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins like fish and poultry , nuts and seeds. It’s important to eat small portions at consistent times throughout the day, avoid skipping meals, pay attention to your hunger and fullness cues and choose water as your beverage of choice. It’s also recommended to engage in resistance exercise to support muscle and bone health and achieve the best results. These strategies may help limit reductions in energy use as the weight comes off. Emerging areas of research Changes in body weight and composition (the amount of fat and fat-free mass in our bodies) play an important role in energy metabolism. articles.content: Physical education should encourage healthy relationships with movement and exercise. (Salah Regouane/Unsplash) In June 2026, the Alberta government released an updated draft of its Grades 7 to 9 Physical Education and Wellness curriculum , intended for optional classroom piloting during the 2026–27 school year and mandatory implementation in September 2027. The way food, bodies and physical activity are discussed in the new curriculum has the potential to prime, endorse or worsen disordered eating and compulsive exercise among youth. Adolescence is a time when youth become more preoccupied with their appearance and experience greater body dissatisfaction . They are also at a higher risk for developing disordered eating behaviours , including dieting, food restriction and binge eating, which can precede eating disorders. Because patterns of dieting and disordered eating in teenage years can persist into adulthood , it’s vital to help young people develop healthy relationships with their bodies. Our research on the conditions that foster eating disorders and body dissatisfaction compels us to speak out and identify the key issues with the proposed curriculum. Health cannot be reduced to weight Throughout the curriculum, higher body weight is framed in relatively simplistic terms, with an emphasis on overeating. For example, one learning outcome states: “Larger portions can lead to overconsumption and increase risk of obesity and chronic disease.” Obesity is a complex, chronic disease with several contributing factors outside of direct control, including genetics, access to physical recreation opportunities and safe neighbourhoods, socioeconomic class and medication side effects. Teaching students that obesity is simply the result of overconsumption risks blaming individuals for their body weight and creating the misleading impression that body size and shape are entirely within their control. Students in larger bodies, or who have family members in larger bodies, are likely to feel blamed and shamed in these lessons. Such simplistic messages can also reinforce weight-based bullying , which is already too common in Canadian schools and has worrying consequences for the health of both victims and bystanders , including an increased risk of eating disorders . Instead of focusing on weight, health education should emphasize behaviours that benefit all dimensions of well-being, regardless of body size. Food is not inherently good or bad The draft curriculum creates a binary distinction between good and bad foods by casting convenient and ultra-processed foods in a negative light. Yet these are inconsistently defined concepts . For example, a Grade 7 learning outcome states: “Modern diets that include ultra-processed foods and convenience foods can be high in calories (energy) and low in nutrients.” Similarly, an outcome in Grade 8 reads: “Compared with processed foods, whole foods harvested from the land absorb nutrients from the soil, enhancing their taste, quality, appearance and nutritional value.” Food binaries attach moral value to food, potentially shaming students who do not have access to the “right” foods. A restrictive, fear-based approach to food can result in out-of-control eating or rigid food avoidance , both of which are forms of disordered eating. These concerns are particularly relevant in Alberta, which is currently experiencing one of the highest rates of food insecurity in the country . Many families rely on food banks, which often distribute processed or convenience foods. Students should not feel ashamed of eating what their families can afford or access, particularly when food insecurity itself can heighten the risk of eating disorders . Instead, students should be taught to approach food intuitively and flexibly based on their access and needs to fuel daily living activities. Tracking food and exercise can backfire Perhaps the most concerning curriculum outcomes are those that ask students to monitor their dietary and exercise patterns and develop personal plans to achieve nutrition and fitness goals and framing “wellness apps” as a helpful resource to do so. Such assignments risk reinforcing the idea that eating and activity patterns are solely within a person’s control. They overlook whether youth have a choice in what food is available in their homes or the privilege of accessing physical activity in safe environments. Evaluating teenagers on behaviours they have little to no control over can set them up for feeling like failures, ashamed or discouraged. Food and exercise tracking are also associated with eating disorders and should not be required school assignments. Despite the widespread promotion of food and exercise tracking tools and apps, research suggests they are relatively ineffective at improving eating and exercise habits and can increase body concerns, disordered eating and compulsive exercise. Wellness apps and tracking devices are not only more attractive to people who have pre-existing eating and body concerns , but can also initiate these preoccupations and disordered behaviours and therefore should not be encouraged in schools. Physical activity is more than appearance The new curriculum risks presenting physical fitness and athletic performance as central reasons for engaging in physical activity. It emphasizes concepts that are specific to muscle building at competitive levels, such as overload, specificity, reversibility and the principle of diminishing returns. Media portrayals of these practices and ideals of muscularity are associated with increased body dissatisfaction and muscle dysmorphia in Canadian youth . Emphasizing these concepts in general health education risks reinforcing a narrow understanding of physical activity centred on physical performance and a preoccupation with muscularity . The language around “personal fitness” could also encourage the idealization of thinness and muscularity as the standard and metric of “health,” rather than teaching students how enjoying movement can create benefits for our bodies, minds, relationships and emotions throughout their lifespan. A broader perspective is needed Physical and health education can play an important role in helping students develop a healthy relationship with food and movement. These topics should not be avoided. Rather, schools need evidence-based health education that is developmentally appropriate, eating disorder-safe, weight neutral , inclusive of those experiencing food insecurity and situated within a broader understanding of adolescent health. For ideas on keeping class discussions weight-neutral and assignments safe and developmentally appropriate, visit the Body Image Research Lab at the University of Calgary, where we research body image, eating disorders and weight bias. articles.content: Canadians aged 65 and older want to decide where they live and most prefer that place to be their current home . The concept of an older adult aging in the place of their choosing emphasizes that preference. Preference, however, does not guarantee that aging in that place will be possible. Feasibility depends on an older person’s circumstances and supports available where they live. John Amagoalik’s story illustrates the gap between preference and possibility when it comes to aging in place of choice. A lifelong advocate for Inuit self-determination and one of the key figures behind the creation of Nunavut , Amagoalik recently spent 16 months in an assisted-living facility in Ottawa after an infection resulted in the amputation of part of his leg. Being more than 2,000 kilometres from Iqaluit, Amagoalik told the CBC, “The worst part was the loneliness.” Friends eventually helped arrange the housing and care that has allowed him to return to his home for now. Although Amagoalik’s circumstances are particular to Nunavut, where some elders must leave the territory to access specialized services not available closer to home , his story raises a question relevant across Canada: What does it mean to say older persons have a choice about where they age if the supports they need are not available where they want to live? What determines where people age As occupational therapists and rehabilitation scientists , our research explores how engagement in everyday activities contributes to health and well-being in later life. Our work has led us to recognize that where people age is shaped not only by their preferences but also by their circumstances and supports around them. For us, this research is also personal. Our mothers continue to live independently, and both chose to move closer to family. Like many with aging parents, we think about what will allow them to continue doing so if their health, mobility or circumstances change. Having a choice about where one lives as one grows older requires realistic options. Rural communities can offer strong social connections and a sense of belonging, but as needs change, limited access to transportation, affordable and accessible housing, and other health and social services may constrain people’s ability to remain in the place they call home. Rural aging and mobility Research on rural aging has described a related tension between “aging in place” and being “stuck in place .” Remaining somewhere does not necessarily mean an older person had a meaningful choice to do so. Transportation provides a good example. Our research with older persons living in rural areas and small towns around Hamilton, Ont., identified considerable reliance on personal vehicles . If few alternatives exist, losing the ability to drive can mean losing access not only to medical appointments and groceries, but also to activities and relationships outside the home. Mobility, after all, is about much more than getting from one place to another. Being able to get around allows us to see friends and family, volunteer, exercise or simply participate in everyday activities that make life meaningful. However, what happens when driving is no longer possible and there is no realistic alternative? If managing your current home becomes difficult, is there help or a suitable and affordable option nearby? Can needed services be accessed without leaving your community? These questions also make us think differently about risk. Risk and what matters Families and health professionals understandably worry about falls , driving safety or whether an older adult can live at home alone . While those risks matter, our research has identified that focusing too much on physical safety can sometimes overshadow what older people themselves value when decisions are being made about where and how they will live. Stopping driving may reduce one kind of risk while increasing risks of isolation and loss of meaningful activities . Moving somewhere with more services may make some aspects of life easier or safer but moving away from neighbours, relationships and a place we call home has consequences for well-being. A home that no longer meets an older person’s needs can carry risk, but so can leaving it. Supporting real choice Planning ahead for mobility changes matters but so do housing, relationships, finances and ensuring support is available. However, people cannot plan around options that do not exist. Supporting real choice about aging in place also means asking: Can older community residents get where they need and want to go? Are housing, health and social supports accessible where people live? When those supports are not available, who fills the gaps? Families, friends and neighbours provide extraordinary support and can expand an older person’s choices but should not be the only infrastructure upon which aging at home depends . Aging in a place of choice cannot simply mean asking older people where they want to live. Communities and governments must ensure people have meaningful and realistic options as their health, mobility and circumstances change. Choice only means something when there are real options. articles.content: Open any news feed from the past few months, and the disasters arrive in a stream: smoke reaching dangerous levels throughout Canada and flash floods in Ottawa , Montréal and Toronto ; heat and drought arriving together on every continent. Driven by climate change, these events are happening more often, and rather than remaining isolated, they cause cascading, interrelated effects. Now enter the “super” or even “Godzilla” El Niño developing in the tropical Pacific. This phenomenon changes weather patterns globally, potentially bringing more extreme heat, drought and flooding. Although it’s a natural climate phenomenon, scientists are concerned about the unprecedented rate of surface warming. The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has declared a greater than 83 per cent probability of strong to very strong El Niño conditions during January to March 2027 . Historical precedents are sobering, with major El Niño events of 1982-83 , 1997-98 and 2015-16 leading to extreme flooding in some regions, severe drought in others, and widespread disruption to ecosystems and economies . Now imagine if hospitals were overrun with respiratory events due to wildfire smoke, migraines, heatstroke and delirium. At the same time, the electricity grid could go down due to overwhelming demand from the use of air conditioning systems. If that scenario sounds plausible, it’s because every element has already happened in Canada, just not all at once. We call these scenarios polycrises, to represent multiple connected crises occurring simultaneously. We’ve seen these before, such as the 2013 Calgary floods , the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic and the 2023 Northwest Territories wildfires that required evacuation. The toll of polycrisis on health care The health-care system deserves special consideration when preparing for polycrises. Canada’s health-care system is over capacity on a normal day, with now-familiar hallway medicine, long wait times, surgical delays, understaffing and insufficient primary and long-term care. Canadian access to care ranked ninth of 10 peer countries in a 2025 study , above only the United States. Now imagine adding severe wildfire smoke, a flood causing energy outages and a new viral illness. It’s easy to imagine health-care access and quality declining. Health care suffers at the centre of polycrises. Wildfire smoke has contributed to 1,900 premature deaths annually and $18 billion in costs in Canada. Evidence shows that smoke increases all-cause mortality and causes exacerbations of cardiovascular disease, respiratory conditions , neurologic diseases like multiple sclerosis and migraines . It can trigger stroke and delirium, affect fetal health and has been associated with developing dementia . During the 2023 wildfires, Ontario asthma-related emergency visits increased by 23.6 per cent . Floods disrupt transportation, supplies and patient discharge, while evacuations overwhelm communities, like when 20,000 Northwest Territories residents fled to Alberta in 2023. Supply-chain interruptions threaten access to medications and medical equipment, as seen during COVID-19. These crises disproportionately affect underhoused individuals , people with disabilities, lower-income households and Indigenous communities . Energy implications A strong El Niño can put the entire energy system under strain, just when the health system is most vulnerable. The effects begin months earlier. Milder winters, altered precipitation and reduced mountain snowpack diminish spring runoff and hydroelectric inflows, leaving reservoirs with less stored energy as summer demand peaks arrive. It can also influence the likelihood of extreme summer heat, which often coincides with periods of low wind output. In June 2026, Europe experienced a heat dome accompanied by a wind drought , reducing wind generation just as soaring temperatures drove up electricity demand for cooling. In extreme heat, solar power has lower capacity – known as derating – losing roughly 0.4 per cent for every degree above 25°C , and dims further under wildfire smoke. Gas turbines also lose capacity to hot-air derating on the hottest afternoons. As with the broader polycrisis, the primary issue is convergence. Demand rises precisely when many supply sources are constrained, leaving the grid with less room to absorb the next shock. The shared patient Energy poverty is where the energy system and health system share a patient. While hospitals have backup power and contingency plans, the greatest risks lie in the community. The households least able to afford cooling, air filtration or backup power are the same populations over-represented in heat and smoke morbidity. British Columbia’s 2021 heat dome led to more than 619 deaths, primarily among the elderly and those who lived in under-resourced communities . The heat dome that fills emergency departments with heatstroke and delirium is the same weather system derating the gas turbines that power hospital wards. The smoke triggering asthma exacerbations also reduces the solar output flowing into the grid. The insulin requiring refrigeration, the elevators in seniors’ residences and the oxygen concentrators in patients’ homes all depend on electricity precisely when demand is greatest. This is the defining property of a polycrisis: interconnected failures that neither the energy system nor the health-care system can prepare for alone. What resilience looks like The encouraging part is that the two systems share their defences as surely as they share their failures. Storage, demand flexibility, interties (transmission links that let grids share electricity), backup power at critical facilities and cooling centres with assured power: every investment that hardens the grid against El Niño-pattern stress also protects health outcomes. One system’s resilience budget is the other’s prevention budget. Energy-affordability support is preventive medicine delivered through a utility bill. The El Niño forecast’s real value is lead time. We must act on this warning and secure backup power, fund cooling centres, bolster critical supply chains and identify patients whose health depends on the grid. The time to prepare for a polycrisis is before the emergency is at our doorstep. This story was co-authored by Luke Killam, co-founder and CEO of GreenKey Energy, an independent energy consultancy. The shared patient Energy poverty is where the energy system and health system share a patient. While hospitals have backup power and contingency plans, the greatest risks lie in the community. The households least able to afford cooling, air filtration or backup power are the same populations over-represented in heat and smoke morbidity. British Columbia’s 2021 heat dome led to more than 619 deaths, primarily among the elderly and those who lived in under-resourced communities . The heat dome that fills emergency departments with heatstroke and delirium is the same weather system derating the gas turbines that power hospital wards. The smoke triggering asthma exacerbations also reduces the solar output flowing into the grid. The insulin requiring refrigeration, the elevators in seniors’ residences and the oxygen concentrators in patients’ homes all depend on electricity precisely when demand is greatest. This is the defining property of a polycrisis: interconnected failures that neither the energy system nor the health-care system can prepare for alone. What resilience looks like The encouraging part is that the two systems share their defences as surely as they share their failures. Storage, demand flexibility, interties (transmission links that let grids share electricity), backup power at critical facilities and cooling centres with assured power: every investment that hardens the grid against El Niño-pattern stress also protects health outcomes. One system’s resilience budget is the other’s prevention budget. Energy-affordability support is preventive medicine delivered through a utility bill. The El Niño forecast’s real value is lead time. We must act on this warning and secure backup power, fund cooling centres, bolster critical supply chains and identify patients whose health depends on the grid. The time to prepare for a polycrisis is before the emergency is at our doorstep. This story was co-authored by Luke Killam, co-founder and CEO of GreenKey Energy, an independent energy consultancy. articles.content: Is that smoothie boosting your immune system or corporate profit? Research found over 96 per cent of immune-boosting content on Instagram to be from creators that sold or advertised products or services. (Unsplash) We all want a well-functioning immune system to help us fight invasive bacteria and viruses and recover faster from illness. Popular “immune-boosting” ideas, however, might be more of a hindrance than a help. Immune boosting is an online trend. Content producers share immune-boosting recipes — from smoothies to soups to poke bowls and pumpkin loaves . Nutrition books speak of “ super powered immunity ” while naturopathic clinics share immune-boosting “tips.” The “boosting” phrase has become so commonplace that it frequently appears in health content from reputable academic institutions . The COVID-19 pandemic — more so than ever in recent memory — had the public thinking hard about immunity . As interdisciplinary public health researchers studying the influential forces that shape public perceptions, the rise of immune-boosting discourse during this time caught our attention. We researched the trending concept in Google search results and on social media sites like Instagram . We found it to be problematic in two ways: First, content often presents scientific inaccuracies about how the immune system functions; second, it showcases corporations that push ineffective products or services. At a time when trust in evidence-based interventions like vaccines is on shaky ground , this can lead to negative outcomes for our health. Immunity and Society is a new series from The Conversation Canada that presents new vaccine discoveries and immune-based innovations that are changing how we understand and protect human health. Through a partnership with the Bridge Research Consortium , these articles — written by experts in Canada at the forefront of immunology, biomanufacturing, social science and humanities — explore the latest developments and their impacts. Balance, don’t supercharge Not all immunity-boosting content is inaccurate or harmful. Information from research or medical organizations often focuses on healthy eating, exercising , getting proper sleep and avoiding the harms of tobacco and alcohol . The idea of boosting or enhancing one’s immunity, however, remains fundamentally flawed. The immune system needs maintaining, not enhancing. That’s because each person’s immune system is complex, made up of cells, tissues, organs and proteins. This system works innately and non-specifically to keep harmful invader germs out, using, for example, the skin and mucous membranes as a protective barrier. It also works adaptively, deploying a targeted and specific response for harmful invaders. The body’s primary immune response. (Wikimedia Commons/Sciencia58) , CC BY-SA The adaptive immune system uses B-cells that produce antibodies — special proteins that attach to invader germs and either mark them for destruction or neutralize their effects. There are also T-cells, which act as destroyers, hunting and killing cells that have been infected by germs . Amazingly, the adaptive process of the immune system builds memory cells of the pathogens it battles. When the same invader re-enters the body, it can be quickly recognized and targeted more effectively. A well-functioning immune system also correctly differentiates between your own cells versus invader cells . An under-performing immune system increases the possibility and severity of infection . But an over-active immune system can lead to a host of autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis. Maintaining the immune system therefore involves balance — not supercharging its functions and abilities. Corporations boost profits Those who promote the concept of “immune boosting” are often simply trying to generate profit. The very idea of “boosting” can create a sentiment of lacking — that one’s health could (always) be better. This frames health status as a deficit requiring people to continually pursue restorative or optimization efforts — a commonly used health and wellness marketing strategy . The first step is to establish a void, accompanied by anxiety or fear. The second step is to offer purchasable actions that address the void. Our research on Instagram during the pandemic, for example, found that more than 96 per cent of the immune-boosting content we reviewed came from creators that sold or advertised products or services. We found 62 different companies tagged in a sample of 28 posts. We also reflected on how the social media hashtag #immunebooster itself functioned as a rhetorical product used to “generate activity in the online attention economy .” Other companies may promote immunity-enhancing products or services with immunity-enhancing claims, such as hydrotherapy , IV drips, cleanses and detoxes . Cereal companies in the past have also marketed their products as “supporting” immunity . There is no good evidence that any of these activities have immune-function benefit. Stem-cell supplements Dietary supplements in the form of vitamins, minerals or herbs also offer limited benefit to those without diagnosed deficiencies. As noted in an immune-boosting article by a Canadian pharmaceutical chain, “to date, no drug, product or natural remedy has been officially approved by Health Canada to boost the immune system.” Yet corporations market them as either explicitly boosting or generally offering benefit to the immune system . Recent research from our team , for example, assessed the marketing of “stem cell” supplements on the e-commerce marketplace, Amazon. We found more than 40 per cent of the products claimed immunity-related benefits. Supplements are now big business, with a market valuation in the hundreds of billions . It is not surprising to find a broad, all-encompassing marketing approach to products such as “stem cell” supplements that have no clear evidence of efficacy for any health ailment Trust in medicine The commercialization of immunity is a concern for all of us. Commercialized health spaces , can damage trust in health-care systems and confusion around who and what we trust . If our perceptions are shaped by companies and influencers , this might negatively influence vital evidence-based health activities, such as vaccination. Rampant vaccine misinformation during the pandemic dissuaded vaccine uptake and helped promote inaccurate ideas of personal immunity . Vaccine hesitancy is highly complex, with multiple factors at play. Politics and polarization are increasingly influential forces . Inaccurate immunity discourse only further clouds information landscapes and, in turn, vaccination decision-making. Health and wellness marketing is savvy and alluring, carefully crafted to pique our interest and provide solutions. In today’s media environments, we all need to be cautious and critical of companies marketing products and services for our health and well-being. It matters when assessing preparedness for any future pandemic , and how our health-care systems can build and maintain public trust. Accurate understandings of immunity help us maintain well-functioning immune systems and a well-functioning society. Alessandro Marcon is affiliated with The Bridge Research Consortium (BRC) Jia Hu works at the BC Centre for Disease Control where his work is focused on on immunizations and vaccine-preventable diseases.

articles.content: After decades of relative neglect, menopause is suddenly everywhere — in the news, on social media and in conversations among friends. Some are calling it the “meno-boom,” and booms attract business. The Canadian menopause wellness market — meaning the products, treatments and services designed and sold to help women manage symptoms before, during and after menopause — is projected to reach a revenue of US$784.9 million by 2030 . But alongside the marketing are sensational claims and outright misinformation , including about how the menopausal transition affects mental health. That’s exactly what my research team has been studying for more than a decade. And as a woman now navigating perimenopause myself, I have a personal appreciation for why these conversations matter. I’m far from being in a minority: the Canadian Institutes of Health Research estimates that about 10 million people in Canada are currently navigating some stage of perimenopause, menopause or post-menopause transition . So let’s cut through the noise. Here’s what the evidence actually says about menopause and mental health. Before you know you’re in perimenopause The increased risk of depressive mood arises early in what researchers call the early menopause transition. This stage is marked by menstrual cycles that are consistently seven days shorter or longer relative to a woman’s usual cycle. Someone whose cycle used to average 30 days, for example, might start having 23- or 37-day cycles. So unless you’re tracking your cycle very closely, it can be easy to miss any connection between mid-life mood changes and perimenopause. It also doesn’t help that depressive symptoms have been shown to fluctuate considerably in perimenopause, making it a moving target. Not just about depression and mood swings Though a lot of research on the menopause transition has focused on depressed mood, there’s growing recognition that other psychological symptoms can show up too. For example, a recent study by our team , following perimenopausal women for three months, found that more than half struggled with moderate-to-severe anger and irritability. Weekly changes in sleep quality, hot flash severity, as well as hormones, predicted weekly changes in anger. Estrogen fluctuation in perimenopause has also been associated with greater sensitivity to interpersonal rejection , highlighting that psychological changes in the menopause transition can involve more than just feeling down. This fits with anecdotes from women that say they just “don’t feel like themselves.” Read more: Perimenopause usually begins in your 40s. How do you know if it has started? Hot flashes don’t explain everything Hot flashes are no fun, and they are extremely common in mid-life, with 60 to 80 per cent of women experiencing them in the years leading up to and following their last menstrual period. But as much as hot flashes may negatively impact quality of life, they don’t fully account for the increase in low mood that we see in perimenopause. For one thing, the timing doesn’t line up . Across the population, mood symptoms begin to increase well before hot flashes emerge. And by the time hot flashes reach their peak severity, depressive symptoms are already declining. At an individual level, this translates to many women experiencing depressive mood in the absence of hot flashes and many others experiencing hot flashes in the absence of mood changes. Hormone therapy isn’t a cure-all Menopausal hormone therapy is highly effective in treating hot flashes and night sweats. Vaginal estrogen cream is also a safe and effective treatment for vaginal dryness and sexual difficulties at any age. The benefits for cognitive difficulties (memory and thinking), sleep and low mood are less well-established. Multiple rigorous trials have confirmed that menopausal hormone therapy doesn’t prevent cognitive decline. And though it has been shown to improve sleep difficulties in women experiencing night sweats, evidence for its benefits in women without these symptoms is less conclusive. As for mood, the overall benefits of menopausal hormone therapy have been found to be quite modest, although some women may benefit more than others. Cognitive behavioural therapy and serotonin-based antidepressants remain the first-line treatments for depressive symptoms, including during perimenopause. Future research may help us better pinpoint who stands to benefit most from hormone therapy. In the meantime, it’s worth keeping both its proven benefits and the limits of the current evidence in view. Not everyone struggles with the transition The increased attention paid to menopause and perimenopause is long overdue, and it stands to greatly improve mid-life care. Women should not have to suffer in silence or go untreated. But we should be mindful about how we discuss it. Women have long been dismissed as “hormonal” — meaning less logical, rational and level-headed than men. Careless narratives or conversations about menopause risk reinforcing that stereotype. Our research consistently finds enormous individual differences in how sensitive women are to the hormonal changes occurring in the menopause transition. For some, rapid shifts in hormone levels can trigger a host of negative mood symptoms. For others, the effects are negligible. Women experiencing difficult symptoms deserve recognition and effective treatment. But mid-life can also bring greater confidence, autonomy and opportunities for personal and professional growth. For some, menopause also means welcome freedom from menstruation and concerns about pregnancy. The “meno-boom” has brought perimenopause out of the shadows, and that’s worth celebrating. But attention isn’t the same as understanding. The research reveals that this period is more complicated (and more individual) than pop culture and business marketing can capture. Taking women’s mid-life mental health seriously means resisting easy answers. Jennifer L. Gordon receives funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR).

articles.content: People who visit emergency departments (EDs) but leave without their care completed are often assumed not to have been ill enough to require that care. However, the high rates of people who leave without completed care is a symptom of the mismatch between the Canadian promise of health care for all and the current capacity of the health-care system. The most profound effects of this mismatch fall on people who are structurally disadvantaged. Our research shows that the people who rely the most on EDs report the poorest care experiences, and often leave without their care completed. This creates a cycle of worsening health and increasing costs. Studying the care experiences of nearly 1,700 patients across three British Columbia EDs, our research team found that people facing the greatest social and economic disadvantages were more likely to report discrimination in the ED, lack access to primary care, depend on EDs for ongoing health problems and rate their care poorly . They were also the most frequent users of EDs. In a different analysis, our research also showed that EDs can significantly interrupt this cycle . Promoting equity Our team at EQUIP Health Care has been researching how to increase effectiveness by supporting health-care organizations to focus on people least well-served by the health-care system. In other words, researching ways to promote equity. Studying primary care clinics that serve people marginalized by poverty, racism and other forms of stigma and discrimination, we identified three key dimensions to doing so: trauma- and violence-informed care , cultural safety/antiracism and substance-use health. We also identified 10 implementation strategies. Our findings showed that patients who received care that promoted equity were more comfortable and confident in their care, leading to increased confidence in preventing and managing their health problems. This, in turn, improved their health outcomes , including depression and trauma symptoms, chronic pain and quality of life. We learned that although education and addressing biases were useful for many providers, inter-professional conversations were needed to develop policy and practices to address racism, stigma and discrimination. We learned that disruption was inevitable and necessary, and that policy change was as important as changes to health-care providers’ practice. More effective care Based on these lessons, we partnered with three B.C. EDs to design an intervention to support leaders and staff to deliver care more effectively. EDs are under immense and increasing pressure, evident in long waits for care and high levels of staff turnover and burnout , fostering a focus on optimizing short-term efficiency. However, the intervention was designed to align with the quintuple aim of health-care improvement , which optimizes effectiveness by enhancing: Patient experiences and outcomes Health-care provider well-being Health equity Service efficiency Health system efficiency Despite significant challenges related to COVID-19 and the worsening epidemic of overdoses and deaths related to the toxic drug supply, staff at two of the EDs mounted intervention strategies. Results showed encouraging trends in patients’ perceptions of the quality of their care and discrimination in the ED, but there were no significant changes in staff sick time. However, most importantly, there was a significant decrease in the percentage of patients who left without their care being completed at the site with the most robust intervention activities. This is crucial because patients who leave the ED before their care is complete often return when their health concerns are more urgent, resulting in significant harms to patients and costs to the health-care system. It’s also demoralizing for staff. We examined how to build on and strengthen these results. Staff and leaders were committed to focusing on those with greatest needs. However, other priorities — such as recruiting and orienting new staff, and responding to escalating crises such as violence against staff, the toxic unregulated drug supply, and COVID-19 — overshadowed their efforts and curtailed the staff and resources needed. Resources and recommendations We identified 10 recommendations for systematically improving care for those who need it most: Initiate interventions within care delivery organizations Conceptualize equity as foundational to health-care quality, not as an “add-on” “Hook” participation by linking equity to the organization’s most pressing “pain points” Seek commitment to effectiveness from leaders across all employment groups Commit sufficient resources to ensure representation from service-users and all employment groups and sufficient leadership and expertise Compose implementation teams of people from all levels and roles, including service-users Assign leadership responsibility to those with leadership roles at executive and clinical levels in alignment with their skills and responsibilities Tailor the intervention to align with the realities of the context Provide some level of education and opportunities for interprofessional dialogue for all Reconsider how time is used to support effectiveness and other elements of the quintuple aim, not efficiency alone To support these recommendations, we created The EQUIP Equity Action Kit , which includes step-by-step directions, assessment and evaluation tools, discussion tools, action tools, videos, animations. We have free on-line courses to support the Action Kit and tools to support the well-being of health-care providers as they face challenging workloads, high stress levels and violence daily. Some resources are available in both English and French. In addition to EDs, many resources have been tailored to other health-care settings such as primary care and cancer care. Colleen Varcoe works for the University of British Columbia, and PreVAIL (Preventing Violence and Inequity Across the Lifespan) a non-profit organization. I have received funding for the research reported in this article from the Canadian Institutes for Health Research and the Public Health Agency of Canada.

Some resources are available in both English and French. In addition to EDs, many resources have been tailored to other health-care settings such as primary care and cancer care. articles.content: Billions of dollars are being spent on research to find a molecule that will cure Alzheimer’s disease. Yet, as Dr. Louis Bherer explains, adopting certain lifestyle habits could significantly reduce the risk of developing symptoms, in some cases by up to half. Dr. Bherer is a professor in the Department of Medicine at the Université de Montréal and researcher and director at the EPIC Centre, the preventive medicine and physical activity centre at the Institut de Cardiologie de Montréal (Montreal Heart Institute). His work focuses on the impact of lifestyle, physical exercise and cognitive stimulation on the brain health of older adults and patients with cardiovascular disease. At his Montréal laboratory, Bherer and his team develop both physical and cognitive exercise programs. The results of their studies corroborate what other research has found on the importance of lifestyle in the prevention of dementia. This factor has been neglected by public health authorities, explains Dr. Bherer, who is also laboratory director at the l’Institut universitaire de gériatrie de Montréal (Montreal University Institute of Geriatrics). We recently spoke to Dr. Bherer: The Conversation Canada : A new Statistics Canada study indicates a substantial decline in healthy life expectancy in Canada. In 2023, it was 66.9 years, a decrease of 3.5 years from the peak of 70.4 years between 2010 and 2012. Are you surprised? Dr. Louis Bherer: Yes and no. But what we do know is that the healthspan-lifespan gap — the gap between life expectancy and healthy life expectancy — is widening. For example, nine out of 10 people have at least one risk factor for cardiovascular disease after the age of 65: being overweight, poor sleep, inactivity, high blood pressure, etc. As life expectancy increases, this means more years in poor health. Our lifestyle is not optimal. Stress and anxiety are on the rise. It’s a scourge. What’s more, people are inactive, they have sleep problems, they are neglecting their diet. We eat quickly, and eat fast food or ultra-processed foods. Although the information is there, and available, we don’t always apply it. Nor do we teach our children to. Physical education should be part of the daily school curriculum, and the basics of nutrition should also be taught. This article is part of our ongoing series The Grey Revolution. The Conversation Canada and La Conversation are exploring the impact of the aging boomer generation on Canadian society, including housing, working, culture, nutrition, travelling and health care. The series explores the upheavals already underway and those looming ahead. For that matter, people are quick to turn to pharmaceutical solutions. The popularity of Ozempic is one example. We want to lose weight, but we aren’t addressing the causes of being overweight. We don’t do much to encourage people to change their lifestyle. It is estimated that nearly half of all dementia cases (45 per cent) could be prevented with a healthy lifestyle. Fourteen modifiable risk factors (FRM) have been identified. TCC: Many people tell themselves: I’m 65 or 70, so it’s too late for me to change my habits. I should have started earlier. L.B.: It’s never too late , even though we know that education (a mitigating factor for dementia) is generally acquired at a young age. This is in contrast to hearing loss, which occurs later in life. Many people do not take it seriously or hide it, yet it’s a factor associated with an increased risk of major cognitive impairment or dementia. And, of course, psychological health plays a major role: a person may be inactive because they feel a little depressed or less motivated, but this increases the risks. We don’t realize that overall health factors are all interrelated. Heart and brain health go hand in hand. What’s good for the heart is good for the brain. TCC: Your laboratory, which focuses on cognitive health, is located at the Institut de cardiologie de Montréal. What exactly are you doing there? L.B.: We use stimulation programs to assess the impact of exercise on physical and cognitive health. Our participants range in age from 50 to 95, with an average age of between 68 and 70. We follow them for periods ranging from three months to a year. They may have mild cognitive deficits that people around them have noticed, and sometimes they suffer from anxiety, a condition that can impact memory and be a predictor of dementia. Other participants have no cognitive issues, but they are at risk due to high blood pressure, diabetes, etc. Our programs include memory games on phones, for example, which improve cognitive function, particularly psycho-motor speed, as well as physical exercises: stationary bikes, treadmills, muscle strengthening, etc. The best approach is a combination of both. TCC: What have you observed? L.B.: We are seeing clinically significant improvements. Participants with mild cognitive impairment may see improvements after six months of training, with differences in their attention, alertness and response speed. They are more alert after just a few weeks. We are also seeing an impact on memory, although this takes longer. Using biomarkers, our research attempts to link the parameters that change, both physically and cognitively, to the effects on the brain. With brain imaging, we can measure improvements in blood flow and brain structures, such as the hippocampus, which plays a key role in memory. Physical training, which participants do three times a week, stimulates the production of proteins that promote neuroplasticity. When muscles work, they produce and release myokines and other exerkines . These molecules play an important role in metabolism, inflammation, bone health and even mood. As we often say, exercise is the miracle pill for overall health. TCC: Many people make profound changes in their lifestyle, but good intentions don’t always last. L.B.: Yes, and that’s a shame, because the positive effects of training disappear within a month or a month and a half. And the older we get, the faster it happens . Ideally, you should choose activities that can be easily integrated into your daily routine. I’m thinking of running, for example, which is a very complete exercise, very easy to do, and inexpensive. Brisk walking is also good, but the idea is to work up a bit of a sweat. And supplement that with some exercises to increase muscle strength and others to improve posture and mobility. This is an important factor in maintaining independence as we age. The fear of falling is a concern for many older people. Balance and posture control exercises, such as yoga, can really make a huge difference to the health and lifestyle of older people.
