articles.content: Cancer is now the leading cause of death in Canada. Two in five Canadians will develop cancer during their lifetime, and one in four will die from it. Every day, nearly 700 people across the country are diagnosed with cancer. According to the Canadian Cancer Society , the most commonly diagnosed cancers are lung, breast, prostate and colorectal cancer. These figures mask a key reality: survival rates vary greatly depending on the type of cancer and, above all, how advanced it is at the time of diagnosis. The statistical data clearly show that survival rates increase when the cancer is detected early. These data highlight the urgent need to improve detection of the disease and, above all, to detect it earlier. A blood test instead of a scalpel This is the context where my research takes place. As a professor of systems engineering at ÉTS Montréal and principal investigator in the cancer research division at the CHUM Research Centre, I am working on liquid biopsy. This approach aims to detect cancer from a simple blood test by analyzing the DNA that tumour cells release into the bloodstream. Unlike conventional biopsies, which require removing a tissue sample from the tumour, liquid biopsy relies on a simple, minimally invasive procedure: a blood test is all that’s needed. The advantages of this approach include reduced pain, lower risks for the patient and less logistical burden associated with hospital procedures. The simplicity of the test also allows for more frequent testing. And finally, unlike many diagnostic procedures, taking a blood sample does not require specialized facilities. Blood can be taken in any health-care setting, whether it’s a local clinic or a community health centre. In medicine, the term “biomarkers” is often used to refer to measurable indicators that provide information about a person’s state of health. The PSA (prostate-specific antigen) test, which has been used for decades to monitor prostate cancer, is a well-known example. Elevated PSA levels in the blood may indicate the presence of cancer, its progression, or a recurrence after treatment. However, the biomarker approach does have limits: PSA is not specific to cancer and test levels can rise for other reasons, which can complicate the interpretation of results. À lire aussi : We designed a new way to build miniature fluidic devices to enable personalized cancer treatment Detecting the invisible Liquid biopsy follows the same logic, but at a different level of precision. Rather than measuring a protein indirectly linked to the disease, it directly detects the genetic traces left by the tumour cells themselves. In this sense, circulating tumour DNA can be seen as a much more specific biomarker, carrying information about the nature of the cancer and its progression. À lire aussi : What adolescents and young adults with cancer want researchers to know The smaller the tumour, the less DNA it releases into the blood. Yet it’s precisely at these very early stages that diagnosis has the greatest impact on survival chances. My aim is to detect these extremely weak signals, sometimes well before the onset of clinical symptoms, or even after treatment, when the cancer appears to have disappeared but may persist in a residual state. Tailoring treatments to each tumour Liquid biopsy also makes it possible to tailor treatments to each patient. By identifying the specific mutations in a tumour, it becomes possible to select targeted therapies that are better suited to the cancer’s genetic profile. This approach paves the way for more precise medicine, which takes into account the biological characteristics specific to each disease. Another major advantage is the ability to monitor the progression of cancer over time. By repeating liquid biopsies before, during and after treatment, it’s possible to observe whether tumour DNA levels are decreasing or increasing. This information can help to quickly determine whether a therapy is effective or needs to be adjusted, thereby avoiding unnecessary treatments and their side effects. When the signal gets lost While liquid biopsy offers promising prospects, it also poses significant technological and methodological challenges. One of the main obstacles is detecting tumour DNA amid a vast background of normal DNA. The mutations we are looking for are sometimes at the very limit of the accuracy of sequencing machines. In my laboratory, we are working to reduce technical errors and develop algorithms capable of distinguishing between a genuine cancer mutation and a false signal generated by sequencing technologies, notably through artificial intelligence approaches. A single blood sample can generate terabytes of data. For each patient, this amounts to billions of DNA fragments to be analyzed, filtered and compared. The management and analysis of this massive data set require robust bioinformatics tools capable of processing the information quickly and accurately. À lire aussi : All for one, not one for all: The promise and challenges of personalized medicine The quality of the analysis also depends on sample preparation. Circulating DNA is often fragmented and degraded. It must be purified, experimental biases must be corrected, and it must be made suitable for sequencing technologies even before the computational analysis stage. A revolution in the making In my view, liquid biopsy represents much more than a technological tool: it is an opportunity to transform the way we detect and monitor cancer. By combining less invasive methods, earlier detection and more personalized medicine, it could improve both patients’ quality of life and their chances of survival. Before becoming standard practice, however, the effectiveness of these approaches will need to be demonstrated in rigorous clinical trials. However, as sequencing technologies advance, what was once the stuff of science fiction is gradually becoming a reality. I am convinced that one day, a simple vial of blood could play a central role in the fight against cancer. He is a member of the Montreal Cancer Institute and a researcher at the CHUM Research Centre. He is named as an inventor on patents, some of which have been licensed for commercialisation by Eurofins-Viracor.

articles.content: Sleep is fundamental to well-being. Decisions to end bi-annual clock changes and remain on permanent daylight saving time (DST) in British Columbia , the North West Territories , Alberta , Manitoba and northwestern Ontario have consequences for many Canadians due to potential sleep disruption. The health risks of transitioning to DST, including increased heart attacks and fatal car accidents , have led most sleep and chronobiology experts , including the first author of this story , to advocate for ending seasonal clock changes in favour of permanent standard time . Governments justify opting for DST to provide later daylight for a range of reasons, including facilitating evening activites , alignment with other areas and promoting health. While permanent DST provides more daylight in the evening hours — something sometimes appealing for those with flexible schedules and access to outdoor spaces — it comes at the cost of later sunrises. Being aware of the potential effects of permanent DST and how to mitigate these will be important for schools. Read more: B.C.’s switch to permanent DST adds to the ‘perfect storm’ for poorer adolescent sleep and mental health Later dawns Due to the short winter days experienced in Canada, dawn will now occur later than the start times for many schools in many of the regions opting for permanent DST. Communities to the north and west within a time zone will have sunrises later than 8 a.m., or even later than 9 a.m. for a sizeable portion of the school year. Grande Prairie, Alta., will see sunrises in December and January after 10 a.m. In the United States, the the Sunshine Protection Act seeks to make daylight saving time permanent . Because winter days are shorter in Canadian northern areas than the more southern United States, the negative consequences of the move to permanent DST will be more profound for Canadians. Why time matters A major concern around choosing the right clock for society has to do with our body’s internal circadian clock. This circadian clock regulates our daily 24-hour rhythms, including our sleep-wake cycles. This clock naturally follows daylight, so as our days get shifted later with DST, our body rhythms also get shifted later . One challenge that many people will face with permanent DST is social jetlag — a mismatch between what our body clock wants to do (follow the sun) and what our school or work schedules expect us to do (follow our alarm clocks). DST worsens social jetlag in two ways. First, DST moves our social schedule an hour earlier relative to dawn. For people with earlier schedules, such as students and teachers, this means waking earlier than our bodies want with the later dawns during fall and winter. Second, later sunsets delay when our bodies want to fall asleep, leading to less sleep overall . Social jetlag also erodes health in several ways, raising rates of depression, cardiovascular disease and metabolic diseases. How a person will respond to permanent DST depends on both their work or school schedule and their chronotype. Those with flexible schedules can adapt their sleep and activity schedules, but this isn’t a luxury afforded to many. Some people are naturally more morning-types (“larks”), while others are naturally more evening types (“owls”). The people who will struggle the most with permanent DST’s late winter dawns are the owls who have early work and school times. This is especially true for teens: Many of the biological changes occurring during adolescence naturally shift the circadian clock later , so teens are much more likely to fall into the “owl” category. Well-being in education and start times As dawn gets later than school start times, communities and families will likely face many challenges. Research from Russia’s short-lived permanent DST suggests detriments for sleep, social jetlag and mood, especially winter depression. Compared to research on the risks associated with DST transitions, there are relatively few studies on permanent DST . Instead, we can look to research on sleep, school start times and student well-being. Teens are considered chronically sleep-deprived because of the mismatch between their circadian rhythms and most school start times. This poses several public-health concerns related to the consequences of sleep loss for daytime sleepiness, attention and executive functioning. Teens’ sleep deficiency is associated with increased engagement in risky behaviours such as alcohol, drug and tobacco use, caffeine use and increased risk for depression, low grades and car accidents. The greater the circadian misalignment, the more likely adolescents are to experience cognitive and school difficulties . This is especially true for teens with ADHD or other health needs associated with sleep challenges. Decades of research points to later school start times being better aligned with adolescents’ circadian rhythms, with benefits for sleep health, mood , attendance , attention and academic performance . It also points to later start times being associated with decreased rates of illness , headaches and mental-health difficulties, including depression and disordered eating . Researchers have also documented improved sense of well-being , reduced caffeine use and reduced risk of motor vehicle accidents . The extensive benefits associated with better alignment of school times with students’ circadian rhythms have led researchers to suggest that later start times could help reduce educational disparities. And it’s not just students who benefit from later start times. Teachers also experience better daytime functioning and sleep health. Mitigation measures Taken together, as sunrise, school start times and students’ biological rhythms become more out of synch, educators can expect more disruptions to students’ engagement and academics. They could also see increased rates of illness (on top of existing seasonal increases) and absences, especially for middle and high schoolers. This is especially concerning given mounting concerns for under-resourced educational systems and unmet classroom needs that leave teachers ill-equipped. Consequences may be greater in rural and remote communities, where school start times tend to be earlier, as in British Columbia . Likewise, social jetlag and associated health consequences tend to be more pronounced in racialized and economically marginalized communities where many people already have earlier start times, less flexibility in schedules, reliance on public transit and high rates of disability and health problems. This brings up important concerns for equity-deserving groups likely to experience greater academic, social and economic detriments associated with permanent DST. As governments enact permanent DST, evaluation related to well-being and safety will be crucial for informing policy and practice. Risks for negative outcomes may also be reduced through various mitigation measures such as public education on sleep health and seasonal mood changes, later or flexible start times, adapting indoor lighting in schools and traffic and pedestrian safety measures. Why time matters A major concern around choosing the right clock for society has to do with our body’s internal circadian clock. This circadian clock regulates our daily 24-hour rhythms, including our sleep-wake cycles. This clock naturally follows daylight, so as our days get shifted later with DST, our body rhythms also get shifted later . One challenge that many people will face with permanent DST is social jetlag — a mismatch between what our body clock wants to do (follow the sun) and what our school or work schedules expect us to do (follow our alarm clocks). DST worsens social jetlag in two ways. First, DST moves our social schedule an hour earlier relative to dawn. For people with earlier schedules, such as students and teachers, this means waking earlier than our bodies want with the later dawns during fall and winter. Second, later sunsets delay when our bodies want to fall asleep, leading to less sleep overall . Social jetlag also erodes health in several ways, raising rates of depression, cardiovascular disease and metabolic diseases. How a person will respond to permanent DST depends on both their work or school schedule and their chronotype. Those with flexible schedules can adapt their sleep and activity schedules, but this isn’t a luxury afforded to many. Some people are naturally more morning-types (“larks”), while others are naturally more evening types (“owls”). The people who will struggle the most with permanent DST’s late winter dawns are the owls who have early work and school times. This is especially true for teens: Many of the biological changes occurring during adolescence naturally shift the circadian clock later , so teens are much more likely to fall into the “owl” category. Research from Russia’s short-lived permanent DST suggests detriments for sleep, social jetlag and mood, especially winter depression. Instead, we can look to research on sleep, school start times and student well-being. Teens are considered chronically sleep-deprived because of the mismatch between their circadian rhythms and most school start times. This poses several public-health concerns related to the consequences of sleep loss for daytime sleepiness, attention and executive functioning. Teens’ sleep deficiency is associated with increased engagement in risky behaviours such as alcohol, drug and tobacco use, caffeine use and increased risk for depression, low grades and car accidents. The greater the circadian misalignment, the more likely adolescents are to experience cognitive and school difficulties . This is especially true for teens with ADHD or other health needs associated with sleep challenges. Decades of research points to later school start times being better aligned with adolescents’ circadian rhythms, with benefits for sleep health, mood , attendance , attention and academic performance . It also points to later start times being associated with decreased rates of illness , headaches and mental-health difficulties, including depression and disordered eating . Researchers have also documented improved sense of well-being , reduced caffeine use and reduced risk of motor vehicle accidents . The extensive benefits associated with better alignment of school times with students’ circadian rhythms have led researchers to suggest that later start times could help reduce educational disparities. And it’s not just students who benefit from later start times. Teachers also experience better daytime functioning and sleep health. Mitigation measures Taken together, as sunrise, school start times and students’ biological rhythms become more out of synch, educators can expect more disruptions to students’ engagement and academics. They could also see increased rates of illness (on top of existing seasonal increases) and absences, especially for middle and high schoolers. This is especially concerning given mounting concerns for under-resourced educational systems and unmet classroom needs that leave teachers ill-equipped. Consequences may be greater in rural and remote communities, where school start times tend to be earlier, as in British Columbia . Likewise, social jetlag and associated health consequences tend to be more pronounced in racialized and economically marginalized communities where many people already have earlier start times, less flexibility in schedules, reliance on public transit and high rates of disability and health problems. This brings up important concerns for equity-deserving groups likely to experience greater academic, social and economic detriments associated with permanent DST. As governments enact permanent DST, evaluation related to well-being and safety will be crucial for informing policy and practice. Risks for negative outcomes may also be reduced through various mitigation measures such as public education on sleep health and seasonal mood changes, later or flexible start times, adapting indoor lighting in schools and traffic and pedestrian safety measures. articles.content: A good and happy life is made in the small connections with others in our communities. (Unsplash) Earlier this year, we convened a meeting of some of the most influential figures in modern happiness research to discuss what they had learned in their 600 combined years of research and professional experience. The group included pioneers like Richard Layard , Sonja Lyubomirsky and Martin Seligman , who turned happiness into a serious science. As a result of their work, 90 per cent of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) member countries are now measuring life satisfaction. Many of these pioneers have remained active into their 80s and 90s, still writing , teaching and mentoring. If any group could identify the ingredients of a good life, this was it. We recently published the outcome of this discussion in the Journal of Happiness Studies . The group identified many central themes to happiness: having basic needs met, relationships, meaningful work and living in ways that align with one’s values and circumstances. Looking ahead, they were concerned about inequalities and declining youth well-being. The single most recurring theme in the discussion, however, was the importance and joy that comes from social relationships. Relationships are the linchpin As an interdisciplinary team of well-being researchers, we expected relationships to be part of the answer. They affect every aspect of life , amplify positive events , mitigate negative events and are considered to be a basic psychological need . This is not only observed in western countries; “having someone to count on” predicts life satisfaction around the world . In short, happy people have strong and satisfying relationships . What we did not expect was how frequently relationships would come up. In nearly every part of the discussion spanning meaning, work, competition, culture, morality, technology and longevity, relationships were the linchpin of happiness. Social engagement is a skill In their personal lives, several of these pioneers deliberately protected time for spouses, relatives, friends or grandchildren. One reorganized a schedule to give their close friendships more room. Another, persuaded by intervention studies , began writing more messages of gratitude , behaving more sociably and trading superficial exchanges for deeper conversations . Social engagement, they suggested, is not a luxury reserved for extroverts or the socially advantaged, but a skill anyone can cultivate . Connection may not always happen on its own, but it often begins with simple acts: taking an interest, reaching out and showing up. These are things we all can do. Their professional lives told the same story. Consistent with the research literature , many pioneers actively built laboratories, departments and collaborations where students and colleagues felt trusted, supported and energized. They saw people do better work when others helped them flourish and they helped others, discovering that others’ success and happiness could add to, rather than subtract from, their own. Relationships help healthier aging Happiness and relationships also offered a plausible link to the unusual longevity represented in the gathering. The scholars did not explicitly agree that their research might have extended their lives, or that any single practice explained their vitality. Still, their own priorities echoed a large body of research connecting close relationships with healthier, happier aging — a finding undeniably witnessed by the Harvard Study of Adult Development . The possibility lingered: Perhaps studying happiness had taught them to invest in the very bonds that helped keep them engaged in life? When the conversation widened from individuals to societies, the relational theme became more urgent. Several participants worried about declining youth well-being , which they attributed to increasingly competitive cultures. Schools rank students against classmates. Universities and workplaces turn peers into rivals. Material comparison makes another person’s gain feel like one’s own loss . Under those conditions, even talented young people can experience education not as discovery or fellowship, but as an effort to survive. Invest in the people around you The group did not deny that competition is part of human life or that it can sometimes spur innovation. But they challenged the assumption that self-interested rivalry is the key to progress. Human beings also survive and thrive through co-operation, social learning and mutual care. They argued that communities organized around a stronger sense of “we” are better positioned to flourish than those trapped in “us versus them.” This is consistent with research on the topic. The moral insight was simple: Your happiness is not my unhappiness. Your well-being can strengthen mine, just as mine can strengthen yours. We flourish by building one another up. The central conclusion was ancient enough to sound obvious but still not always easy to follow in our fast-paced society. A good and happy life is not constructed alone. It is made in the small connections with others in our daily lives, the workplaces we humanize, the rivalries we refuse, the communities we build and the society we all shape. After hundreds of years of combined research, the pioneers’ most compelling insight was simple: Invest in the people around you. articles.content: When Canada legalized recreational cannabis in October 2018, one concern was that more legal stores would make cannabis easier for young people to access and encourage adolescent use . But does having more cannabis retailers near high schools actually mean more students use cannabis? Our study suggests the relationship is more complicated. Across more than 419,000 student survey responses collected in four Canadian provinces, we found little consistent evidence that greater access to nearby cannabis retailers was associated with whether adolescents used cannabis. However, accessibility was associated with more frequent use among existing users during the first year of legalization. Our research team examined this question in a study published in the Drug and Alcohol Dependence journal . Our findings offer new insight into how cannabis retail accessibility relates to adolescent use as Canada’s legal market matures. Retail accessibility and cannabis use We examined student survey data collected between 2018–19 and 2023–24 through the COMPASS study in Alberta, British Columbia, Ontario and Québec. We measured accessibility using the distance to the nearest retailer, the number of nearby stores and a measure that gives greater weight to closer retailers. Overall, greater retail accessibility was not consistently associated with ever using cannabis, past-year or past-month use, or daily and almost-daily use. Cannabis use also declined in our study sample. Past-year use fell from 22.2 per cent in 2018 to 10.0 per cent in 2023. Past-month use declined from 13.0 per cent to 6.4 per cent, while almost-daily use fell from 4.2 per cent to 2.4 per cent. These figures describe students in participating schools, not a nationally representative sample. For national context, Health Canada’s Canadian Student Alcohol and Drugs Survey reported that 18.3 per cent of students in Grades 7 to 12 used cannabis in 2023–24. This estimate comes from a separate survey and should not be directly equated with our findings. One important exception emerged among students who had already used cannabis. In 2018, greater retail accessibility was associated with more frequent use. This association weakened and was no longer statistically significant in subsequent years. Proximity may have mattered for frequency of use early after legalization, but it did not remain a consistent predictor. Store proximity may not tell the whole story Adolescents do not necessarily obtain cannabis directly from legal retailers. They may access it through friends, family members or other social connections, so the distance between a school and a store may not reflect how easily young people can obtain cannabis. Research on American high school students has identified friends as an important source of cannabis, whether through sharing or purchasing it. This research helps explain why the distance between a student’s school and the nearest cannabis retailer may not reflect how easily they can obtain cannabis. However, our study did not examine where students obtained cannabis, so access through friends is one possible explanation for our findings, not something we directly tested. Other factors, including peer influences and perceptions of risk, may also affect use. Our study cannot establish which factors explain the findings. What does this mean for cannabis policy? Our findings do not mean adolescent cannabis use is harmless or that governments should abandon safeguards. Research has linked adolescent cannabis use with health and educational concerns. A meta-analysis found associations with depression and suicidal ideation, while other research examined associations between cannabis use and poorer academic outcomes. A 2024 systematic review also examined cannabis retail availability and health outcomes, underscoring the need to consider different populations and outcomes rather than assume store proximity affects everyone in the same way. Restrictions on how close cannabis stores can operate to schools may still serve important purposes. However, our findings suggest that store proximity alone may be insufficient to understand or prevent adolescent use. Prevention efforts may also need to address social access, peer influences and factors associated with frequent consumption. Our study has limitations. Cannabis use was self-reported, and we surveyed students across successive years rather than following the same people over time. We measured retail access around schools, which may not reflect where students live or spend their time. The COVID-19 pandemic also disrupted school and social environments during the study period. The number of cannabis stores near a school is easy to measure, but it is only one part of a larger picture. Understanding adolescent cannabis use requires looking beyond store locations to consider how young people obtain cannabis, why they use it and how to prevent harmful patterns of consumption. articles.content: A Victorian-era séance. (Pearson's Magazine, 1910) In November 1857, during a séance in Jersey City, the medium Leah Brown claimed her body produced luminous particles . So intense was the luminosity emanating from her, she recalled in her memoir , that it almost burned her hands. She rinsed her hands under a tap and then pushed them into the damp earth outside. The following evening, luminous particles were discovered in the soil where she’d pressed her hands. They were later identified as phosphorous. In her memoir, Brown admitted to the presence of phosphorous but insisted her body had produced it. She further claimed that the manifestation of spirits in the body naturally produced “phosphoric lights” and the particles came naturally from her body. She added that mediums’ bodies could produce phosphorous and implied that they were part of what was then known as ectoplasmic remains — the viscous, gauze-like substance historically claimed by 19th- and 20th-century spiritualist mediums to exude from their bodies during trances. In truth? She’d probably secretly brought phosphorus with her and had used it in the séance. But her account shows how phosphorus was used in séances decades ago — and provides a glimpse of the chemistry behind making the dead seem visible as Halloween approaches. The dangers of phosphorous White phosphorus, also called yellow phosphorus, gives off a faint light as it slowly reacts with oxygen in the air. The effect is chemiluminescence, light from a chemical reaction — it’s not evidence of supernatural energy. In a dark room, the glow could indeed be rather uncanny and convincing of a phantom presence. Phosphorus is not a safe chemical. It’s toxic if swallowed and inhaling the fumes too can be harmful. It’s unclear whether those living in the Victorian era knew about these dangers or if they had any knowledge of the dangers of phosphorous. White phosphorous was used in “strike anywhere” matches , and many people — mostly women — working in factories where it was used developed a disease called phossy jaw . It affected teeth and jawbone. Certainly, long-term factory exposure is not comparable to séances, and we don’t have any definitive evidence of mediums suffering from this disease, but what’s relevant here is that white phosphorus was a known industrial poison and yet it was used regularly for seances. Nonetheless, a glowing ghost was not always a toxic ghost. In 1910, the magician William Marriott demonstrated how spirit hands could appear with some props and luminous paint. In 1877, William Henry Bailman’s luminous paint used calcium-sulphide and became a major commercial success. This compound could absorb light and glow in darkness . Ties between sciences and spiritualism Historian Richard Noakes’ work has shown physical sciences had a difficult yet symbiotic relation with spiritualism. Bailman’s paint is an example that ghost-making was part of a broader culture of chemical experimentation. In 1874, William Crookes, a renowned chemist, investigated self-luminous objects at séances. He specifically tested phosphorised oil and phosphorous lamps to see if he could understand the process better. Yet Crookes did not dismiss spiritualism as complete hoax. His writings suggest sciences and spiritualism were not completely separate worlds, and their methods sometimes overlapped. It’s important to examine the role literature played in understanding the link between phosphorus and ghosts. The most famous literary example of the use of phosphorus for ethereal spectacle comes from Arthur Conan Doyle’s The Hound of the Baskervilles , where the dog is treated with phosphorous to create the ghostly effect. Doyle’s work had profound impact on the development of forensics . The fictional use of phosphorous to create a spectral hound very likely brought more attention to the use of phosphorous within the spiritualist community. Ironically, the Scottish author had a keen interest in the paranormal and wanted to believe that ghosts existed. It’s strange how the creator of world’s most popular rational detective — Sherlock Holmes — was so deeply invested in the supernatural. Disposable bodies More recently, British author Laura Purcell’s Gothic novel, The Shape of Darkness , deals specifically with mediums and their use of phosphorus. Purcell’s novel is about a poor child medium who is unaware that the glow in her body is because of phosphorous and imagines that the burn she feels is because of the spirits. Her father is suffering from phossy jaw from his work at a match factory, and the book focuses on the inescapable nature of poverty and how the child is now the family’s only source of income. In both Purcell’s novel and The Hound of the Baskervilles , toxic phosphorous is used on subjects without any agency. The victims, a dog and a child, suffer health hazards just to create a supernatural phenomenon. Both these works of fiction give voice to a very real issue — some bodies have always been considered more disposable than others. Our Halloween decors today are filled with spooky things that glow. But once upon a time, a mysterious glow held the promise of extraordinary proof that the dead had returned for those gathered in darkness. Séances claimed to dissolve the boundaries between the dead and the living. And while we may continue debating whether ghosts are real, that spooky light in the dark decades ago was certainly not supernatural. articles.content: AI adoption in medicine is accelerating: more than 12,000 primary care clinicians have enrolled in Canada Health Infoway’s national AI scribe program , about 5,000 Ontario physicians use AI scribes and roughly one in five Canadian physicians now use AI tools. Almost 60 per cent report a cut in administrative time. AI scribes are tools that, with the patient’s consent, listen to a clinical visit and automatically draft the physician’s notes. We’re writing as an emergency physician who has led digital transformation in emergency departments for six years and advises on AI readiness (Ali Abdalvand), and an organizational psychologist studying burnout and responsible AI adoption (Ehsan Etezad). Our observation is that AI keeps its narrow promise of saving time. But without proper frameworks, it quietly adds new burdens that absorb those savings. We believe the fix is organizational. Burnout stems from mismatches in workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values; not from any single task such as paperwork. One study found electronic health record design and use accounted for just 6.8 per cent of the differences in burnout between clinicians. When work conditions such as a chaotic atmosphere and lack of control over workload were also considered, that number rose to 36.2 per cent. In emergency medicine , physicians are interrupted 7.9 times an hour, and prescribing error rates nearly triple with interruptions. No scribe changes that. How AI quietly adds to physicians’ work I think we can all relate to the idea that when you complete one task efficiently and save some time, new demands fill the space, making it seem as though nothing was saved in the first place. But as AI introduces new ways of reducing the time physicians spend on documentation, it comes with novel ways of adding work, too. The time dividend gets spent. Saved time rarely comes back to clinicians. In Canada’s national AI scribe program , half of clinicians put the time they saved into other administrative work, and one in five used it to add appointments. Studies from the United States show the same pattern: AI scribe adopters across five health systems saved 13.4 minutes of daily EHR time and delivered 0.49 more visits per week. Errors do happen and patient safety is at stake. In two simulated tests , Ontario’s auditor general reported that most of the 20 government-approved AI scribes made errors. Twelve recorded the wrong drug, nine invented treatment steps and 17 missed key mental-health details in at least one test. The province says there are no known reports of patient harm. OntarioMD, a subsidiary of the Ontario Medical Association that helps physicians adopt digital health tools with funding from the Ontario Ministry of Health, responded that physicians “know they must review every clinical note generated by their AI scribe.” That safeguard is essential — and it is also work. Used to be authors and now editors. Automation often leaves humans the hardest job, which is watching for rare but serious errors. When physicians at one U.S. health system got AI-drafted replies to patient messages, replying time did not decline as physicians still have to edit the text to make sure it was accurate. More tools, more switching. In our experience, many AI tools sit outside core clinical systems. As an example, in one of our emergency departments, starting a night shift means logging into the work station, the health record, the dictation system, the imaging viewer, the EKG viewer and, most recently, an AI scribe; six systems before seeing the first patient, and a copy-and-paste at the end of every interaction because the scribe lives outside the chart. Thirty-nine per cent of Canadian physicians named better-connected, interoperable systems as a priority. Always learning because it’s always changing. Keeping up with constant learning is a job demand in its own right and it can wear people down. This is also known as AI fatigue , defined as the overwhelming pressure of keeping up with AI tools for people’s jobs. Change fatigue is a predictable response to how change is managed by the health-care system and health-care leaders and it is not a reflection of someone’s failing to learn or to adapt. A better way We propose a practical framework that can be used by health-care organizations to improve the adoption of AI. This framework, GRACE, was co-developed by one of the authors, Ehsan Etezad, and it sets out five principles for moving toward responsible adoption. GRACE framework for responsible adoption of AI. (Ehsan Etezad) , CC BY Govern adoption . Include front-line clinicians on AI committees. Give every pilot a stop-rule written in advance. If the pilot doesn’t return measurable time, or audits find errors above an agreed threshold, it ends or is redesigned. Respect autonomy . Keep use voluntary and let clinicians choose among vetted tools. Respecting autonomy is an essential component of responsible AI adoption. Advance access. Build tools into the core clinical record so no one has to copy and paste. Fund access fairly. Cultivate competence. Offer protected, paid learning time and peer “AI champions.” Evaluate effectiveness. Track burnout, after-hours work, note accuracy and whether time actually comes back. Another practical tool, the AI Adoption Matrix, maps organizations on two dimensions. Enablement is how broadly people can access, use and build skills with AI. Governance is how well policies, oversight and accountability work. We encourage health-care organizations to map themselves on this quadrant and work toward being “Responsible Pioneers” with GRACE. We encourage health-care organizations to map themselves on this quadrant. (Ehsan Etezad) , CC BY The real test There is increasing pressure to move fast with AI adoption in health-care systems and it will likely continue. We would like to clarify that we’re not arguing against adoption of AI in health care. We actually encourage it and are excited about the future it will bring to all of us. That said, we encourage health-care organizations to adopt AI responsibly because stakes are high in medicine and patient safety could be at risk. We believe success should be measured by how happy a physician can feel at their job and about their job, not just how many patients they can see in one shift. None of us wants our loved ones to be treated by an exhausted and overwhelmed physician, so let’s ask ourselves how can we reimagine a health-care system that won’t burn out our physicians. Ali Abdalvand is the chief medical officer for Elewana Advisory, a consulting firm specialized in health-care digital transformation. He is also a founding director of Western MedTech, a non-for-profit society focused on supporting health-care innovators. Ehsan Etezad provides private consulting at MEUS Science with a focus on Leadership & Culture, Responsible Adoption of AI, and Psychological Health & Safety.

articles.content: For older adults with dementia or Parkinson’s disease, staying hydrated can be more complicated than simply drinking more water. Dehydration can occur when fluid intake is insufficient, the body loses too much fluid or both occur together. This problem is widespread. A review of studies found that about one in four older adults outside of hospital settings experience dehydration due to insufficient fluid intake. In Canada, a study of more than 96,000 Ontario long-term care residents aged 65 and older found that approximately one in six experienced dehydration during the study period. When an older person becomes dehydrated, the advice seems straightforward: drink more water. But people with brain disorders, including dementia and Parkinson’s disease, may need help putting that advice into action . Drinking is partly a brain-regulated behaviour : the brain detects changes in the body’s fluid balance, generates thirst and helps translate that signal into the behaviour needed to seek and drink water. Research involving people with Alzheimer’s dementia suggests that cognitive impairment may weaken their protective thirst response, reducing their ability to recognize and respond adequately to the body’s need for water. People with dementia may also forget to drink. Similarly, older adults with Parkinson’s disease may struggle to drink enough because of swallowing difficulties , even when they recognize thirst. Dehydration can, in turn, worsen confusion and impair thinking . Why bladder health matters Canadians are becoming increasingly aware of the importance of keeping their brains healthy and resilient to age well, not simply to live longer. A growing body of research shows that lifestyles that include a rich social life, frequent physical activity, eating a healthy MIND (Mediterranean-DASH Diet Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay) diet and doing new and challenging things like cooking new recipes are important in keeping our brains healthy. Yet, one aspect of protecting our cognitive functioning that is often neglected is maintaining our bladder and urinary tract health . Preventing urinary tract infections (UTIs) is a key part of keeping our brains healthy as we age. How the risks of UTIs relate to brain health While we typically think of UTIs as relatively minor infections, the health risks are not the same for all populations. UTIs are common, with more than 150 million people affected globally every year. While these infections are common in young sexually active women, seniors over the age of 65 also experience higher risk. The incidence rate then increases further after age 85. UTIs present differently with age. UTIs are more common among the elderly, yet are often missed due to atypical symptoms . In younger populations, the classic UTI symptom is a burning and/or painful sensation when urinating. Older adults may not show classic UTI signs . Sudden behavioural changes or changes in personality are important reasons to seek assessment. These can be indicators of UTIs in older adults, and can include mental fog, confusion, mood changes, extreme fatigue, balance problems and/or falls, loss of appetite, and new or increasing incontinence. UTIs can cause inflammation. If unrecognized and untreated, this inflammation can impact the brain and cause cognitive decline. The risk is particularly high for those already suffering from brain disorders such as Alzheimer’s dementia and Parkinson’s disease. People with dementia are more likely to be dehydrated, and dehydration increases the risk of urinary tract infections . Risk of dehydration is high for those in long-term care. It’s important to know that in older patients, UTIs can trigger delirium — a sudden change in attention, thinking and awareness. This delirium is often interpreted as part of dementia rather than as a symptom of a possible UTI, which can lead to delays in seeking treatment. And even more concerning, a growing body of research suggests that the impact of infection-induced delirium is not necessarily temporary. Research published in Alzheimer’s and Dementia discusses how UTI-related delirium “ accelerates cognitive and functional decline .” The study’s senior author, Dr. Shouri Lahiri, describes a “vicious cycle” in which dementia patients are at greater risk of infectious, while the delirium that accompanies infection contributes to cognitive decline. Preventing dehydration and UTIs in seniors Practical ways to prevent dehydration and UTIs in seniors include: • Offering water and other drinks throughout the day , rather than waiting for them to ask. • Paying attention to whether they’re actually drinking. • Helping them use the toilet regularly and making it easier for them to find and reach the bathroom. Respond patiently to accidents and assist with personal care while respecting their dignity. • Seeking prompt medical assessment for sudden, unexplained confusion or changes in alertness or behaviour. These changes can have several causes in which UTI could be one. Caregivers play an important role in noticing sudden changes in behaviour, alertness or thinking. These changes should prompt medical assessment rather than being dismissed as aging or dementia. Nurses and doctors should investigate the cause and decide whether urine testing is needed. articles.content: In early September, Conservative Party MP Dean Allison held a four-day independent, unsanctioned “inquiry” for “Canadians to share their personal experiences of injuries…from the COVID-19 vaccine(s).” The event heard testimony that alleged the response to COVID-19 was “a miserable failure,” not least due to the “assaults on freedom and other malign actions.” An opinion piece in the Toronto Sun subsequently claimed that COVID-19 vaccine programs “killed thousands of Canadians,” repeating a call for an immediate stop of COVID-19 mRNA vaccinations, as well as “resignations, arrests and a full public inquiry…by the prime minister.” It further claimed that Canada’s COVID-19 vaccination efforts represent, at best, the “biggest health policy mistake in Canadian history.” But testimony heard at this inquiry — and responses to that testimony — conflate factual claims with ethical claims. As a consequence, it fails to recognize the ethical factors critical to understanding and justifying COVID-19 vaccination efforts. As public health ethicists, we’re interested in clarifying the factors necessary to substantiate claims about “policy mistakes” and informing expectations for future vaccination policy decisions. The conflation of facts and ethics Some of the claims made in the Allison inquiry and related reporting pertained to facts, both stated and omitted. Other claims were ethical in nature. The difference is critical to understanding and justifying COVID-19 vaccination efforts. For example, questions of facts are: How many people were injured or died as a result of COVID-19 vaccination How were vaccine candidates tested and regulated How many people were saved by vaccines . Immunity and Society is a new series from The Conversation Canada that presents new vaccine discoveries and immune-based innovations that are changing how we understand and protect human health. Through a partnership with the Bridge Research Consortium , these articles — written by experts in Canada at the forefront of immunology, biomanufacturing, social science and humanities — explore the latest developments and their impacts. Getting on the same page about these facts and dispelling mis- and disinformation remains crucial. For example, the Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) records 455 reports of deaths following COVID-19 vaccination, noting these deaths weren’t necessarily attributable to the vaccine. After assessing causality, PHAC reports a total of four deaths consistent with causal association to immunization. To put this in context, more than 100 million COVID-19 vaccine doses have been administered in Canada. But getting on the same page about facts is not enough. That’s because claims about whether the government is justified in imposing certain obligations or burdens on the public — for example, requirements that citizens get vaccinated — are not answerable by facts alone. These are questions of ethics. These claims are about what one should do or what governments have legitimate authority to do, morally speaking: in other words, what is considered good or right or just. Values and policy decisions Such ethical claims are a matter of values, which people or groups may prioritize differently. For example, in deciding on health policy options, some may prefer the option that preserves personal autonomy above all else. Others may prioritize fairness and the policy option that minimizes deaths or health disparities. And some may locate the preservation of autonomy in policy options that are fair for all and that saves lives. Critically, no policy decision is ever free of values and value judgments. All policy decisions, including those related to vaccination, involve trade-offs of competing values. That necessarily means there will be trade-offs in the distribution of benefits, risks and burdens experienced across individuals and groups in society. While evidence can tell us what those benefits, risks and burdens might be, it cannot by itself tell us what the right trade-off is. That is, whether it is ethically justifiable to limit autonomy in some ways in order to preserve autonomy in others or to protect certain segments of the population from severe illness or death. In other words, facts alone will not determine how those competing values should be balanced, what outcomes matter the most and whose interests should be prioritized, among other things. Discussions about the legitimacy of Canada’s COVID-19 vaccination efforts or determining whether it was the “biggest health policy mistake in Canadian history” requires not only solid scientific facts, but also explicit ethical reasoning. This entails careful analysis of the values at stake, how trade-offs may reasonably be made between those values and ultimately what governments are ethically justified in doing in the name of public health. The ethics of imposing risk Fundamentally, the nature of the ethical claims made throughout the Allison inquiry and relevant reporting relate to one’s freedom to choose whether to be placed at risk by taking the COVID-19 vaccine. Yet, as our research argues, such claims about vaccine risks often fail to acknowledge or attend to the reciprocal nature of those risks and the reciprocal nature of freedom . At the same time that we may be exposed to risk when getting vaccinated (since no medical intervention is entirely risk-free), we also impose risk on others by choosing to forgo vaccination or choosing policy options that fail to effectively address vaccine-preventable diseases. Just as having the freedom to engage in an activity necessarily entails accepting some of the risks that are created in doing that activity, imposing risks on others can correspondingly justify limits being placed on one’s freedoms. A useful example is driving a car: Choosing to drive means accepting risks to one’s own safety, and it also imposes risks on other road users. Those risks to others can justify restricting the freedom to drive at high speeds by imposing and enforcing speed limits. The existence of risk alone doesn’t preclude governments from implementing policy or health interventions. Every choice carries risk, including the choice not to act. While vaccines themselves do entail some small risks, they are used to reduce a much greater risk of disease that people may not be able to avoid or mitigate on their own. Vaccination policies are not implemented against a backdrop of zero risk, and so doing nothing — such as choosing not to introduce vaccination policies — also creates risk. In certain situations, such as pandemics, it can create more risk, and governments should be accountable for these risks as well. Some of the statements made at the Allison inquiry and in corresponding media coverage appear to hold that governments cannot impose risk on the public. From an ethical standpoint, this is not a given, especially when action and inaction both involve risk. Such claims need further ethical analysis and reasoning that examines the nature of the risks and benefits, how they are distributed and the strength of the justifications used to defend policy action or inaction. Greater attention to ethics in policymaking and evaluation is critical to help identify the values at the heart of policy prescriptions, including related to freedom and risk, and to separate factual uncertainty from disagreement about those values. Only then will we be able to have constructive discussion about vaccination and vaccine policy in Canada. Maxwell J. Silva and Kari Pahlman do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: The fire that swept through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright over the weekend in Alberta killed four soldiers and injured 39 people, including 19 reported in critical condition. The thoughts of Canadians are with the families, the military community, the people of Wainwright and the responders who answered the call. But what happened after the fire deserves attention too. Wainwright’s hospital became a triage hub for what the town’s mayor described as the largest mass casualty event the community has ever seen. Patients were also transferred to hospitals in Edmonton, Calgary and Red Deer. The response mobilized 22 ground ambulances, six airplanes and two helicopters . The Canadian Armed Forces relies on civilian systems for specialized services and mass casualty events . Civilian health readiness is therefore part of national defence. Thirteen months before Wainwright, Canada rehearsed the challenge of a casualty surge . Its findings deserve action. A system with little slack The response to a mass-casualty event does not play out in an otherwise empty health-care system. It competes with everyday care for staff, beds, transport and supplies. The Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI) reports that hospital beds increased by only four per cent between 2014–15 and 2023–24 as Canada’s population grew by 13 per cent. Beds per capita fell by seven per cent. These national figures don’t establish Alberta’s capacity on the day of the fire, but they show why having enough infrastructure, staff and expertise is so important. Alberta has two burn centres, in Edmonton and Calgary . That specialist capacity is an asset. But rural hospitals need staff, supplies and transportation to stabilize severely injured patients and move them safely to burn centres while continuing to serve their own communities. Canada’s health-care system sits at the centre of what’s known as a polycrisis : several systems are under strain, each situation compounding the other. Read more: ‘Polycrisis’ may be a buzzword, but it could help us tackle the world’s woes Climate change is prolonging wildfire seasons. Inflation is squeezing budgets and supply chains. Workforce shortages are persisting after the COVID-19 pandemic . The flu season is surging. The consequences of these crises affect health system response and care. Wainwright is experiencing its mass casualty event amid this ongoing polycrisis. The question is whether any system can absorb the next shock while still dealing with the last. What Canada already learned In September 2025, 79 people from health-care systems across the country, federal agencies and the Canadian Armed Forces gathered in Toronto for Exercise Canada Paratus . Paratus assessed overseas casualties, but the lessons apply to all hazards. Led by key disaster management teams and leaders, the exercise simulated about 100 casualties a week arriving in provincial and territorial health-care systems in Canada from a war in Europe. The post-exercise report is blunt. Three findings are relevant to planning after Wainwright: • Capacity: The report identified workforce challenges and the need to expand infrastructure, staffing and expertise for sustained casualty surges. • Patient tracking: Canada has no integrated system to follow casualties as they move between military and civilian care. At Wainwright, the injured were dispersed across several hospitals within hours. • Governance: The report called for a federal–provincial–territorial health emergency and security authority with clear leadership, roles and decision rights. At the moment, there’s no organization co-ordinating health-care system capacity across federal, provincial and territorial governments. Health care is defence infrastructure NATO already recognizes the link between healthcare and defence. One of its seven baseline requirements for national resilience is the ability to manage mass casualties and disruptive health crises, including functioning civilian health systems and secure medical supplies . Canada’s allies already treat health-care systems as strategic infrastructure, alongside energy grids and supply chains. At the 2025 Hague NATO summit , allies agreed that up to 1.5 per cent of GDP within their new five per cent defence spending target could support resilience, including civil preparedness. Finland’s comprehensive security model treats health security as a vital societal function , while Sweden’s total defence approach recognizes healthcare as essential to defence . Canada should seize this opportunity to make a clear case for health investments that strengthen defence readiness. 5 steps Canada must take Canada already has the diagnosis. As the polycrisis deepens, sudden events like Wainwright will keep exposing the cost of failing to fill gaps. Here’s how Canada should respond: First, implement the Paratus recommendations with a public timeline. Second, create the permanent federal–provincial–territorial health emergency body the report calls for. Third, build patient tracking that works across civilian and military care, so every casualty can be followed from the scene to recovery. Fourth, treat surge capacity, including rural hospitals near bases and critical infrastructure, as a defence-relevant investment. Finally, make the next national exercise a domestic, sudden scenario that applies a sudden mass-casualty event onto a system already under strain. New tools, including AI-enabled polycrisis simulation, allow authorities to rehearse these compounding scenarios before they happen; they’re already being developed . The clinicians and paramedics who responded at Wainwright were part of Canada’s defence capacity, regardless of whether we call them that. Paratus asked whether our health system could survive intact if war came to us from overseas. Wainwright answered a harder question: what happens when the emergency is already here. articles.content: Conversations about sex after illness, disease or the onset of disability tend to stall on the same question: How far does the sex you’re having now fall short of the sex you used to have? That comparison can make it difficult to imagine what satisfying sex might look like when pain, fatigue, reduced mobility, changes in sensation or difficulty holding certain positions make familiar sex harder to sustain. Some people keep trying to reproduce the sex they used to have. Others withdraw from sex altogether. Sexual scripts are cultural and interpersonal routines that guide who initiates sex, what activities follow and how it should end. Traditional ones tend to centre penile-vaginal intercourse as “real sex,” and everything else is treated as tangential — a warm-up or an afterthought. Adapting to these changes tends to require sexual flexibility — a willingness to explore new and different ways of experiencing sexual satisfaction , pleasure and intimacy. Sex toys can help facilitate that shift. Used as accessibility tools, they can deliver controlled stimulation, reduce the physical effort sex requires and broaden what satisfying sex can involve and look like. From taboo to useful toolkit For many years, sex toys were associated with films like Secretary and Fifty Shades of Grey , or with alternative sexual lifestyles. Now, the tide is turning. Media and public discourse increasingly present sex toys as positive, adaptive tools. Netflix’s How to Build a Sex Room , for example, and the popularity of affordable products such as the viral “rose toy” , point to growing normalization. Accessibility begins with choice: for one person, adapting might mean trying out a clitoral vibrator with air-pulse technology. For another, it might mean adding a pillow to make certain positions more comfortable. Making the decision to purchase a sex toy can be daunting, and choosing the right one isn’t always easy. Many tools are expensive, come in conspicuous packaging or are simply too loud. And some may not be safe , like those containing chemicals that can disrupt hormones. Tools that do the heavy lifting Sex toys have real potential to function as sexual health aids that support satisfaction and pleasure at every stage of life. Vibrators are among the most familiar sexual aids. A recent nationally representative study of 1,170 women found that 50.6 per cent of Canadian women have used one before. But the category is broader than the word suggests . Vibrators range in function, design and where they offer stimulation, from wands and rabbits to discreet clitoral and bullet vibrators. There are many options for different preferences, and design can really matter for accessibility. Models with ergonomic handles may be easier for someone with limited grip, while hands-free toys can remove the need to hold a device in place, which can be quite useful when disability or fatigue makes repetitive movement tiring. Vibrators can also provide stimulation when sensation is reduced, help close the orgasm gap and create opportunities for self-exploration . Read more: The orgasm gap and why women climax less than men Of course, vibration is not necessarily for everyone. For some, it may help to start at a low intensity or to use a toy over clothing. Other tools redistribute sexual effort in different ways. Sex swings, wedges, adaptive seating and even ordinary pillows can support body weight, which may benefit people with limited hip movement, paralysis or joint pain. Sensory play — sex involving blindfolds, whips, paddles or restraints — can also help expand intimacy beyond genital stimulation. And if vaginal dryness is an issue, lubricants can help make sexual exploration more comfortable. By and large, supportive-care oncology research shows that combining sex toys with adaptive practices, such as mindfulness and expanding one’s definition of sex , can improve sexual satisfaction, desire and relationship quality. Likewise, studies have shown that clitoral vibrators benefit women with multiple sclerosis or spinal cord injuries and can improve pelvic-floor and sexual functioning more generally. Where access breaks down For those with disabilities, there are additional barriers that increase the challenge of cultivating a satisfying sex life. Alongside stigma and assumptions that disabled people have little or no interest in sex comes limited provision of sexual health information about pleasure and adaptation. Privacy is also limited for those living with family or receiving support at home, which constrains masturbation and the practical business of acquiring and storing a sex toy. However, there are resources that can help. Platforms such as OMGYes illustrate the range of ways tools can be used to adapt sex. Sex therapy is also a beneficial way to learn about how to adapt sex and improve sexual relationships. Sexual satisfaction should not depend on following one dominant sexual script. With ongoing communication, attention to consent and safer-sex practices , sex toys can help cultivate forms of intimacy that respond to changing bodies across the lifespan. articles.content: Rats are on the ballot in Canadian municipal elections this fall, with several political parties promising to tackle city rat problems . While rats may seem like a niche election issue, they can point to broader societal concerns about housing, public services and civic engagement. Rats are ubiquitous urban residents that cities have attempted to evict for centuries . Often portrayed as dirty pests and bringers of plague, they can harbour pathogens that cause illnesses to people and pets , like rat bite fever and leptospirosis . So why have cities had so little success in reducing rat numbers? Well, rats are synanthropes , species that benefit from living alongside humans, and have adapted remarkably well to our paved, cacophonic and bustling streets. Cities provide abundant resources for rats to thrive : food scraps are meals; standing water on sidewalks supplies drinking water; and cracks in buildings offer access to shelter. Municipal policies and bylaws shape how these environments are built and maintained, influencing living conditions for both people and rats. Thinking about rats through municipal elections can offer a more tangible way to understand how complex it is to manage rats without addressing broader issues. We reviewed studies from high-income country cities. Using synthesis and complex systems mapping methods, we examined the social and environmental conditions linked to urban rats, how they influence where people encounter rats across different neighbourhoods and how they impact residents’ ability to respond. Here are a few of our findings and how they connect to municipal issues, using examples from Vancouver’s upcoming election. Habitability, affordability and security Our homes are the most intimate spaces where we can encounter rats. Adequate housing is a human right enshrined under many nations’ laws, including Canada’s . Housing habitability, affordability and security — components of adequate housing — can impact encounters between residents and rats. Concerns about “ living in housing that doesn’t meet [people’s] needs ” refers to habitability — or the quality of housing that guarantees safety and protection against threats to health. Cracks and gaps in older, poorly maintained dwellings allow rats into places where people eat and sleep . Infestations can contaminate food and are linked to anxiety, depressive symptoms and worries about health . Household rat allergen exposure is associated with increased asthma-related health-care issues, including among children. Affordability matters, too. When housing costs leave little money for other essentials due to people “ paying more than they can afford ,” residents may be unable to pay for measures to prevent or remediate rat infestations, adding financial strain to households already facing competing needs. Housing insecurity is also central to why some residents might be more impacted by rats than others. For example, renters may be more likely to experience sustained rat infestations. Fear of eviction or landlord-tenant conflicts can discourage renters from seeking help. Landlord inaction can leave tenants living with persistent infestations and little power to act. Commitments to strengthen tenant protections could reduce barriers in resolving these problems by holding landlords to the city’s maintenance standards . This bylaw requires owners to eliminate pest infestations and maintain their properties to prevent pest harbourage. Unhoused populations may be at higher risk of rat contact. In Vancouver, the number of unhoused people increased 12 per cent between 2023 and 2025, a general trend mirrored across Canada Prolonged periods outdoors, alongside limited sanitation access , can also increase contact with rats. This speaks to candidate concerns that “ in a wealthy city like Vancouver, people are sleeping rough .” Yet city councils have some power over housing supply . Municipalities play an important role in land use policy and regulations, which matter for reducing rodent exposures through availability of safe, stable housing. Waste, sanitation, neighbourhood conditions Cities are hubs for consumption and waste like trash, food scraps, and sewage. Missed garbage pickups and dirty streets are more than a nuisance, they’re also culprits of ratty conditions. Previous studies have linked rat problems with dog waste and human waste . These findings connect to candidate criticisms like “ city streets and parks are covered with animal and human poop .” In fact, open defecation is an ongoing urban issue related to housing insecurity and limited public washrooms. But, when it comes to waste and rats, not all neighbourhoods are the same . Conditions and resources that support rats and residents’ ability to address them vary across neighbourhoods, with infestations often occurring in neighbourhoods experiencing long-term disinvestment and structural marginalization . Civic engagement So how do municipalities know where to target interventions? Many cities use municipal 311 services to understand how rats are distributed across neighbourhoods. They also capture resident concerns to draw municipal attention to problems affecting everyday life. When it comes to rat management, 311 aligns with pledges for “ a City Hall that listens ” and seeks “ involvement of local residents .” However, rat studies acknowledge the limitations of these data in their current form: residents differ in access, ability, knowledge and trust to report to 311 systems . So, while 311 services can be channels for civic participation and a pragmatic way to monitor and manage rats, they can also reflect broader social inequities . Beyond the elections The real work is done after voting day comes and goes. Luckily, Vancouver, like numerous other cities, already has a Healthy City Strategy that aligns with proactive and equitable rat management. This approach prioritizes determinants of health — including housing, sanitation and access to protective resources — by addressing root causes and directing resources to where barriers are greater. For rat management, this means identifying where infestations and conditions that sustain them coincide with limited resident resources to respond. So, the next time you see a rat scurrying along, perhaps you’ll think about what rats symbolize — not just dirt and disease, but our everyday urban living. Kaylee Byers is co-lead of the Vancouver Rat Project and collaborates with the Chicago Rat Project. She receives funding from Michael Smith Health Research BC (Scholar Award). She holds a Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada Discovery Horizons Grant and MITACS Accelerate funding for research on urban rats.

articles.content: When you seek medical care, you hope that your doctor will present you with treatment options that are proven to be effective for your condition, that harms do not outweigh benefits and that recommended treatments are affordable and account for your personal situation. But if your doctor has been influenced by messages, payments or gifts from drug companies, that is unlikely to be the case, as our team from Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States found. Pharmaceutical industry promotion is a global phenomenon. In the mid 2010s, companies in the U.S. spent just under US$30 billion annually to convince doctors to prescribe their products. Figures in other countries are harder to come by but in the mid 2010s, close to CA$500 million was being spent in Canada on advertising in medical journals and on sales representatives who visit doctors’ offices. Between 2015 to 2024, 17,519 Australian doctors received AU$148.7 million from pharmaceutical companies for conferences, travel costs or consultancy fees. In 2020, seven of the top 10 largest pharmaceutical companies globally spent more on marketing than on developing new drugs . Our research examines the relationship between pharmaceutical promotion and doctors’ prescribing. Evidence shows the effects of promotion Our Cochrane systematic review looked at the results of 93 studies involving millions of doctors and published largely over the past two decades. Due to their rigour, Cochrane reviews are considered the gold standard for evidence synthesis. We examined what happens to the appropriateness, quantity and cost of prescriptions when doctors accept payments or meals from the pharmaceutical industry or rely on pharmaceutical representatives for their education or prescribing information. We looked at the effects of a range of types of promotion: advertising and industry-sponsored education, gifts such as free meals and payments for consulting or advisory board membership and free drug samples. The result is not good news for patients. Doctors who receive gifts or payments prescribe less appropriately and issue more prescriptions — and those prescriptions tend to be more costly. Exposure to pharmaceutical advertising or education probably increases how many prescriptions a doctor issues and may increase costs and decrease appropriateness. The evidence on the effects of free samples is less clear, as there were fewer studies. We also looked at whether conflict-of-interest policies make a difference. Some medical schools and hospitals have policies limiting interactions among students, trainees or doctors and the industry, such as banning sales visits or specific types of gifts. The result is more appropriate prescribing and possibly fewer prescriptions. The longer the exposure and the stricter the policies, the greater the effect. Greater exposure to promotion has greater effects The more company-sponsored meals that doctors ate and the more gifts or payments they received, the more their prescribing deteriorated. The more expensive the gift or the higher the value of the payment, the worse the outcome on prescribing. A meal worth as little as US$20 led to more prescriptions for the drug made by the company providing the meal. With each additional meal, doctors issued more prescriptions. Disturbingly, given the legacy of opioid addiction and deaths from overdose, the more meals from opioid manufacturers doctors received, the more opioids they prescribed . ‘I can’t be bought for the price of a sandwich’ Doctors recognize the commercial motivation behind industry’s interactions with them, but do not believe they are affected . Comments to the effect of “I can’t be bought for the price of a sandwich” are a common refrain. Our results convincingly demonstrate those denials cannot be justified. Most doctors who interact with drug companies are not being bribed; companies do not require prescriptions in exchange for gifts. Clinicians are affected through the “ gift relationship .” Receiving a gift of any kind or size, whether wanted or unwanted, creates an obligation — often unconscious — for individuals to repay what they have received. Michael Oldani, a former sales representative who is now a medical anthropologist who researches pharmaceutical marketing tactics, describes the central role played by the gift relationship in an ethnographic analysis of the influence of sales representatives on prescribing. Promotion also provides a reminder that focuses clinicians’ attention on promoted products so they’re more likely to think of these products when making a prescribing decision. From transparency data to public health action The extent of our review is possible because of a recent large expansion in research on pharmaceutical promotion due to the implementation of the 2013 Physician Payments Sunshine Act in the U.S., and other similar national transparency databases that record payments from drug companies to doctors. The Sunshine Act alone includes payments to more than a million doctors. Another database records the several million prescriptions written by these doctors. Combining these databases offers significantly more data, allowing for the identification of more precise associations between payments and prescribing. That includes showing that the greater the exposure, the greater the effect. Our findings reinforce why pharmaceutical promotion must be addressed as a commercial determinant of health — a key pathway through which corporations negatively impact public health. Commercial determinants of health have been defined as “the systems, practices, and pathways through which commercial actors drive health and equity.” Commercial determinants play a key role in the obesity epidemic, the rapid global growth in noncommunicable diseases and the climate emergency. Our review convincingly settles the debate about the effects of promotion on the way that doctors prescribe and shows that promotion is likely to be a major commercial determinant of (ill)-health. The medical community and governments can no longer ignore the consequences of the promotion of medicines on prescribing. It is time for strong concrete action to be taken to put an end to the way that companies are allowed to influence doctors. He has received funding from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research in the past. Alice Fabbri is currently working as a public health physician at the Hygiene and Public Health Unit in Ravenna, Department of Public Health, Azienda Sanitaria Locale (AUSL) Romagna, Italy. Barbara Mintzes receives funding from the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC). She is an expert witness for Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration, and has acted as an expert witness for Health Canada. Dr Mintzes is a member of Association Mieux Prescrire and Health Action International and is General Secretary of the International Society of Drug Bulletins (ISDB). Quinn Grundy served as consultant for the Government of Canada Competition Bureau in 2025. Dr. Grundy has received research funding from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the Social Science and Humanities Research Council, the World Health Organization, and the Greenwall Foundation, a not-for-profit bioethics research foundation. Dr. Grundy serves as Director of the World Health Organization Collaborating Centre for Governance, Transparency, and Accountability in the Pharmaceutical Sector.
